Mr. Speaker, the subject before us is a Very important one, and will, no doubt, receive careful consideration at the hands of Parliament. We have heard a great deal about the comprehensiveness and sufficiency of the report brought in by the committee. I would have been surprised if such a committee, with such a head, had brought in anything but a comphehensive and somewhat satisfactory report. If I have any criticism to make with regard to the conduct of the committee it is that they *sat too long. Perhaps it was difficult to finish the business in a shorter time, but seven or eight weeks is rather too long for a committee to sit. It takes practically eight weeks out of our sessions-which are long enough, goodness knows-and it cuts short the time for consideration of whatever report may be brought in. Perhaps I had not the ability to be named on this committee, but I regard myself as fortunate in escaping it. I was not on that committee; and if I had been, 'I would not_ say that I could have got, through the work more quickly. If,'however, I had any advice to give to a committee man, it would be to endeavour to select his subjects, that is, to select his witnesses, and if he can get three or four men who can tell their story in the right manner and to the extent that is . necessary for the purposes of the committee, that is all that is necessary. In that way a great deal of time could be saved in the committee and more time left in the House to discuss the necessary details in putting a report of this kind into effective shape.	*
The hon. member for York South (Mr. W. F. Maclean) says that it would be de-

sirable to deal with this question expeditiously and to make an end of it. I would agree with him to a very grea/t extent in that if it could be done. Certain classes we could satisfy, or we could at least tell them that that is all they are going to get, and that is the end of the matter, but there are only comparatively few of that class. On the other hand, we have on our hands a large body of men with whom we cannot deal in that way, men who are more or less maimed, some of them being 95 per cent incapacitated, others being 100 per cent incapacitated. We have also large armies of women and children on the hands of the Government and the country. Conditions vary from time to time, from year to year, and sometimes from month to month, and there must be an authoritative body to deal with those men, women and children in the different stages as they move along. Of course, they drop out as they die; the children drop out as they come of age and the widows drop out as they get married, or other changes take place in life. But there ig a floating population, a stream of people walking alongside of us with whom we must keep in touch and of whom we must take care all along. That being the case, it is impossible to carry out in its entirety the proposition of the hon. member for York South that we should reach a conclusion, cut the thing off and be done with it. I do not say that in any harsh sense. I know the hon. member is anxious to deal in the most generous and best way with everybody who was concerned in the war. We all have a desire to get rid of troubles if we can, and we would get rid of any troubles of this class just as quickly as we could, but there is no use making the attempt because we have to look after the interests of those soldiers while they continue to require our assistance. So much for that.
The amendment that is before the House this afternoon is a very important one, one which deals specifically with the fishermen of this country. It is difficult to get in this country anybody who does not belong to some class. He is a very peculiar man whom you can single out by himself and say: He is alone; he does not belong to a class. I think it is a safe proposition to say that" everybody belongs to some class or another, and if you do anything for any soldier you are possibly doing it for a man of that classs. I am not trying to make a proposition of dealing with a class easily; but when we segregate the soldier into classes we try to get them into the largest groups and to deal with the largest groups.

The farmer is possibly the largest group which went overseas, although I am not sure about that. The miner is a very large and extensive group; the lumberman is a large group, and the fisherman is a large group. I have no doubt the fishermen would be one of the large groups, and if we are going to deal with fishermen, we are dealing with them because they belong to a large class of people in this country. They are important people, good citizens, who have done their part in the war, who are a producing class, men who become heads of households, who have a family around them, who have a little stock of implements requisite for carrying on their trade. Besides that, as a rule, you find a fisherman with a little bit of a farm whenever he can get one and with a few cattle, doing the best he can to support his family. You also find him assuming the responsibilities of citizenship in whatever part of the country he lives. He is just as much a colonizer as a farmer. True, half a dozen farmers spread along the country-side, each with a farm, make a big showing, much more if you take 20, 30 or 50 of them and spread them along the country-side iwith farms. On the other hand, if you take 20 or even 50 fishermen and put them into a little village toy the seaside where they follow their avocation of fishermen, they do not make .much of a showing. I am going to leave them as a class because they do not require any advocacy on my part. Their standing in the country is as Safe and high as that of any other class that we have. I have only one other commendation to make of the fishermen. When my right hon. friend (Sir Robert Borden) was running his election in 1911, not then burdened with the responsibility of being a Prime Minister, but having a fair hope that the goal of his ambition was not far distant, he singled out in this country one class of people who were the apple of his eye, upon whom he set his affection, and he .said: "IP I should ever come into power, there is in this country one class of people which, above all others, I should like to safeguard and protect and carry along safely, metaphorically speaking, in my arms, and those men are the fishermen. The right hon. gentleman told us then that if he should ever get into power he was going to apply for medical care and attendance for the fishermen of Canada. Of course, he did not do that, tout that is always understood. The heart was there; the good intention was there, and if he did not look upon them as

the best class of men to single out for this great benefit to foe conferred upon them; if they rwere not the class of people deserving of that, he would not have so singled them out. With all the other deserving characteristics of the fishermen of this country, I have to their credit this one thing which no other class of people in Canada has obtained from so high an authority as the Prime Minister. Whoever else will vote for this amendment if it comes to a vote, I feel confident that, in view of past opinions which the Prime Minister has held of the fishermen of Canada, he will not go back on his record and do anything but vote for this amendment and do the very best in the interest of the fishermen. I leave the question of the fishermen there to speak for itself.
There are occasions when I ram influenced by certain hon, gentlemen in the House.
I am delighted to foe able to vote with the hon. member dor Skeena (Mr. Peck). Almost every Scotchman is an admirer of another fighter, and I must say that I have the greatest possible admiration for the hon. member for Skeena, not for any political side that he may foe on because, at present he is on the wrong side, but for other excellent [qualities which he possesses.
I am still hopeful that, when things mix up a little and when he gets his bearings again, he may wander to some more congenial clime than where he now chooses to eet himself.
This amendment [would foe particularly embarrassing for me if I had any notion of voting against it-I -may say I have not- because the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon) is the seconder. For that reason I shall foe -able to give undivided and unquestioned support to this amendment when it comes -to a vote. There is another reason, which is close to the heart of every man, -and that is one likes to give any cause a second chance. There -will be a second opportunity, if the amendment is adopted, for the committee to gather up the details in this matter and deal with it briefly. Some hon. -gentlemen say it would take too long. There is no -reason why it should take long. The facts are all before the committee, and if the committee -chooses to change their report, they can do so in half an hour. If they decide against changing it, that is an end of the matter.
There is another part of the committee's report which I wish to bring to the attention of the House, and that is the part dealing with vocational training. It has been brought to my notice that those who are engaged in the different courses of vocational training in this country are not satisfied with the hearing they received before the committee. I do not believe that is the fault of the chairman, or possibly the members of the committee. However, the fact remains that a large body of men who are receiving vocational training, particularly in the province of Ontario, and who were promised, I am told, that they would be called upon to appear before this committee to give evidence when the proper time came, were not called. The committee wound up its business and made its report without giving these men an opportunity to tell the committee what they thought should be done in their ease. It is a great mistake for any committee, or even a judge or jury, dealing with returned soldiers not to give them the greatest possible opportunity of presenting their case and consider it in the most careful way. After that is done we must, of course, maintain that stability of judgment which should characterize us all, and deal with every subject upon its merits and within our powers. But we should not let it be supposed that we pre-judge a case, or reach a conclusion too quickly and refuse to give the men affected the fullest opportunity of presenting their case. I have here a statement prepared in writing. I am always timid when approaching the reading of a document in the House for fear I might be called to time, but I hope for the sake of saving time I shall be permitted to put this statement on Hansard so that the Prime Minister and the Government, and everybody concerned with the conduct of vocational training and soldiers' civil re-establishment may see it. What these men have to say, for I make no secret of the fact that this document which I hold in my hands was handed to me by gentlemen who are concerned about the matter of vocational training, is briefly this: Vocational training-and this is news to me is -conducted -differently in the province of Ontario from other provinces. The province of -Ontario, possibly to the pride of the province, have insisted upon conducting this educational work themselves. It is only to-day that I discovered that while the bare machinery of conducting these schools -the appointment of teachers, and so forth 

belongs to this Federal Government, the real substance of the work is carried on under the supervision and control of the Government of Ontario. I understand they

took this position because they
5 p.m. insisted on provincial rights. They insisted that vocational training was education, and that being education, it came within their jurisdiction. They have maintained that position and I am told that the work is being done very well by the province, that, if anything, it is being done better in Ontario than in other parts of Canada. Let me as briefly as possible go over the few facts I have here, just by way of presentment of the case to the Government, with the hope that they will give the matter consideration. Whether this report is referred back to the committee or not, there will be an opportunity for the Government to put something in the Bill that will be of assistance to those who are receiving vocational training, if they think proper so to do. If I were in any other position than that of presenting the case of returned soldiers
I would possibly feel that I was imposing on the House. But this is the case of returned soldiers who say that they were told to go before the committee and tell their story and that afterwards they were sent word that they need not come, that their case was not going to be heard. They accordingly take this indirect way of asking a member of this House, my humble self, to take advantage of the presentation of this report to bring the .matter up and thus give them an opportunity of telling their story. This will go on record and the chairman of the committee, the minister in charge of this department, and everybody else who is in any way concerned about the welfare of these men receiving vocational training will have an opportunity of reading the story from their standpoint. The facts should be before Parliament and be- * fore the officials of the different departments concerned. I hope these various men who were subpoenaed to appear before the committee but who afterwards were not given the opportunity of telling their story will be called into the department and that the minister who is in charge of vocational training will give them the fullest possible opportunity of saying what they have to say and provide whatever remedies they are entitled to. I repeat to the Prime Minister and to the Government that it is highly necessary that every possible attention should be given to any cases of this kind, so that whether we can give money or whether we can give the things that we should give, one thing we will always give and that is a respectful hearing and a sympathetic ear to whatever these men have to present. They are entitled to it and I am sure there is no justification for a lack of attention when these men present their views on this very important subject. With the presentation of this matter and hoping that it will receive careful consideration and that whatever action is necessary may be taken, I will say again that I am in favour of classing the fishermen of this country as being amongst those who are entitled to receive consideration.
I am in favour of including the fishermen of this country in the classes that are entitled to receive consideration. I think it was the hon. member for Frontemac (Mr. Edwards) iwho said that the fisherman cannot give the same security for the loan as the farmer. I do not quite agree with that. The fisherman would only require a small loan, the farmer gets a big one, and I submit to the Government that the security of the fisherman for a email loan, is just

as good as the security of the farmer for a large loan. I am not finding fault with the farmer who goes on the land. We give him land, we give him cattle, we 'help him to build a house-our money going to all of these purposes, and some of his own I suppose. Then he gives a security on what we have provided for him and we hope that it will !be successful security and that he himself (will be successful in his operations. That is the postion of the farmer. The fisherman builds a boat, constructs .a little wharf, and equips himself with nets and whatever else is necessary for him to carry on fishing. The Government could take security on everything he has and lend him a few hundred dollars in order to start him up. In a very short time he would be able-if he has any luck at all-to pay that money 'back, because the turnover in fishing is very much more rapid than it is in farming; and I am quite confident that, taking the proportion of the two loans and taking the character of the security dn each case, you will get just as good security from the fisherman proportionately as you do from t'he farmer. I am not saying that the farmer is less deserving of help than the fisherman. I say that both should be helped; and every returned soldier in this country that is willing to work, and produce, and support his family, should, within reasonable bounds, he helped. Along those lines I trust t'he committee will have another turn at this report, and, excellent as it now is, that they will give it a little polish that will reflect the face of the fisherman smiling, bright and happy.

As I assume my hon. friend from Skeena will press his amendment to a division, and as I apprehend that no matter how an hon. member may vote on this question he is liable to be misunderstood I want to say a word or two by way of explanation of how. I, at any rate, shall vote. I shall support the report of the committee because of what it contains; I cannot see my way clear to oppose it because of what it does not contain. As my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Caldwell) pointed out this is in the first place a very practical parliamentary question at this stage of the session. We have a committee which has drawn up a report as to which I should like, if time permitted, to repeat all the complimentary things which have been said of the chairman. In the drawing up of that report the committee have spent weeks of arduous and unremitting toil and in effect they say to the House: Having regard to the financial
	*
condition of the country Which we have carefully gone into and having regard to the present claims of one particular class oi the community, we do not feel that we can go further, as a pensions committee, than in suggesting, what all of us admit to be, most substantial advances, bringing what Canada has done for the disabled, and the dependents of the dead, into the front rank of the relief which has been given by any belligerent country. Now my hon. friend from Carleton, N.B., has told us on his authority as a member of the committee, that even if this report did go back to them at this stage of the session, he is perfectly confident that they have gone into the work so thoroughly the report would not be altered in the sense of the amendment. So I am brought to this position: If I voted for the amendment I should be showing for the returned soldier that of which he has had a very great abundance but which does not do very much for him; I should be showing sympathy, but there would be no possibility, or no probability, of giving him practical help. That is the practical Parliamentary question to settle; and I feel that so much pains have been taken with this report, it carries us so much farther on the road which we shall travel- believe me, Mr. Speaker,-for some time in this country, that I could not take the responsibility of running any risk about making immediate progress to the point that the committee has recommended.
Now, turn for a moment to the merits-

I (would like to ask -my hon. friend a question. Has he not repeatedly voted to defeat the Government, and had he succeeded would he not have prevented the good ,work of the committee and the advantages of this report from having been brought in?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
I have the very great difficulty in answering my hon. friend's question in that I did not hear a word of it. If my hon. friend will repeat it in a louder voice I will do my very best to give him as courteous a reply as I know how.
Turning to the merits of the question, 1 draw a sharp distinction in regard to an argument which has been touched upon by several hon. gentlemen. I draw a sharp distinction between farmers dealt with under the Land Settlement scheme, and fishermen or any other class of the community. Let me say in regard to the amendment in the first place that I do not think its drawing is very happy in this connection. The amendment asks us to give

subsidies to fishermen the same way that we have done to farmers. Well, Mr. Speaker, if I understand this question, -we have not given any subsidies to farmers; we have given loans to farmers, so that I take it my hon. friend would regard my criticism of the wording of the' amendment as well placed.
The object of the amendment is for aid to be granted in the way of loans, not subsidies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
If that is what the hon. gentleman means I will not go. any further in criticism of the wording of his amendment. I was saying, Sir, that I draw a sharp distinction between farmers dealt with under the Land Settlement scheme and the fishermen or any other class in the community. I was perfectly clear in my own mind-listening to the discussion on the Land Settlement scheme when it was first introduced, as I have on every subsequent occasion it has been before the House -that the intention of the Government as expressed by the Minister of the Interior was to give help to soldiers, it is true, under the Land Settlement scheme, but their first and most primary consideration was that that scheme was a fine thing for Canada. In that view I thoroughly concurred, and the Land Settlement scheme has had my modest benediction since its inception. Sir, I used an argument in the remarks I addressed to the House on the Budget, supported by figures, which went far, in my judgment, to show that it is upon the development of the land, upon the possibilities of agriculture, in this country, that we depend not only for our financial success but for our financial solvency in the years that are immediately before us; and I said in the original debate on the Land Settlement scheme that I supported it not in the view that it was any great benefit to the soldier to begin with-and I spoke from considerable experience of what he is up against and what he has to go through-but that in my judgment, considering the fibre of the men we were going to have on the land, it would be a splendid thing for the whole country. That I think differentiated the farmer from the other classes concerned not so much in quality as in degree. The fisherman-to the extent that he pr <-duces-of course benefits the country just as much as the farmer does; but we must consider what are the possibilities in the way of developing certain industries, what are the financial results to come out of the support of those varying industries, and I
contend that my differentiation is well taken in that regard.
Now, that brings me to the consideration that after all, Mr. 'Speaker, in regard to a loan we are reduced in the last analysis to the elementary fact that two parties are concerned-one is the lender, the other is the borrower; and if the lender has nothing to lend, the borrower naturally goes out of the question, and the lender keeps out. We have the assurance that up to the present time, with the expenditure on the land settlement scheme and the other immense expenditures involved in the aftermath of the war, the country is strained to the utmost possibility of its finances. Faced with that condition of affairs, I come to the argument which I think is absolutely sound, that if you consider the case of the fishermen you must consider also the case of the man who wants to start a small business -in a word, you must consider any other class in the community who may have reasonable claims on the Government, the Parliament, and the people of this country for their war work. And if we considered this amendment we should be undertaking the first step in a whole series of financial commitments which would lead us to a point where I do not think the finances of the country could stand the strain. That is how the question looks to me up to the present moment.
There is only one point I have further to make, . Mr. Speaker, and it is this. I do not take it that the report of the committee closes the door on further consideration of any soldier's case. I modestly offered to the House when the question of subsidies was up before a suggestion along the lines of my hon. friend from South York (Mr. Maclean), which I would have accompanied by the consideration that both parties to the bargain would regard the matter as closed-

Hear, hear.
Mr. MICHAEL CLARK -which received at that time very scant support in this House, and later very scant support from the committee. I fear that for the moment that suggestion has gone by the board. But I want to repeat that I do not vote for the adoption of the report of the committee on the understanding that it closes the question of the returned soldier. We shall not be able to close it, .because we may be sure that it will crop up in various shapes in the years to come. But I do repeat that we have gone a long way for the moment.

Now, there is the practical consideration which I wish to offer to the Government, if I may do so, in regard to this matter being closed. I tried to find out from my hon. friend the ex-Minister of Militia while he was still in office-but he told me the work was not really in the Militia Department-whether the Government had accurate statistics as to how many returned men are now reasonably placed in this country. What occurs to me from time to time, knowing my own immediate surroundings in Alberta, is that most of the sons who have happily come back to their homes are continuously and profitably employed on the farms from which they went to the war. I want to say to my hon. friends of the Government in very good faith and with very great earnestness, that I think it would greatly facilitate the work of Parliament and of this Government in future appeals that are made to us if an endeavour were made through some department to get accurate statistics as to how many returned men are placed, and how many there are yet to place. So that I think in the recess -which I trust we shall approach sometime between now and Christmas; rather near midsummer than Christmas, I hope-inquiry might very well be made along that line, and the Government* might endeavour to furnish themselves with information which would be helpful to us in future appeals to this House-or to some other House with a much changed personnel.
As I see the question up to the present moment, I have in the brief period-in the ordinary acceptation of the adjective brief-put my views as well as I know how before the House, and I shall vote with a clear conscience for the report.

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. SIR ROBERT BORDEN (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I think there is a good deal of merit in the contention put forward by my hon. friend (Mr. Clark), as to the importance of exact statistics so far as they can be obtained with respect to the present occupations of men who went overseas to fight in pursuance of their duty to. their country. There is much to be said for that contention, and I am not certain whether the committee whose labours have been so prolonged have given any consideration to the importance of such statistics or to the means by which they could be obtained. For the moment I can only say to my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Clark) and to the House that I shall commend his suggestion to the 'attention of the Minister of Militia and to the attention of the Min-

ister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and I hope that the House may at the earliest available opportunity have the information which has been asked for.
So far as the motion itself is concerned, no one can deny that it demands the most attentive consideration, and that for two reasons. In the first place, it concerns the report of a committee which for nine weeks was engaged in as active and laborious work upon the questions committed to it as was ever performed, I think, by any committee of this House. And I desire to associate myself most'unreservedly with all that has been said in appreciation of the work of the members of the committee, and especially of the work of the chairman and vice-chairman. Then the motion is also deserving of our closest attention because it has relation to men who fought overseas and who belong to a class whose occupation is of the highest advantage to the country as a whole, who are distinguished by their zeal and industry in that occupation, and who are deserving of every possible consideration that Parliament and the country can give to them.
I find, however, that the question involved in the amendment has been dealt with in the report of the committee and has been carefully considered by that committee. They say in their report:
As was more fully set out in the Report of last year, financial assistance in the form of loans or grants has been suggested for the benefit of a great variety of classes of returned soldiers whose needs covered almost every possible activity.
And after enumerating some of these, including fishermen both on the coasts and in the inland waters, university students, and those who desire loans for the purpose of re-paying mortgages or other indebtedness on their houses, or of buying or erecting homes in which to reside, and various other classes, the committee say in conclusion:
The difficulty which faced your Committee was the conviction that a grant to any particular class or classes, no matter how worthy or pressing their needs might be, must inevitably result in the widest extension of a system of loans for all and every .purpose of re-establishment.
No concrete, workable plan whereby such a general system of advances could be safely adopted has been suggested, and your Committee feels unable to recommend any scheme which could equitably supply the demands of the many whose suggestions have been brought to its attention.
Now, we referred this question to a strong and very representative committee of the House, and I think we are all agreed that

the labours of that committee have been intelligent, zealous and indefatigable. The member for North Cape Breton and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie) presented a very extraordinary argument; he said that he would like the committee to have a second chance. Well, that principle if carried out to its logical conclusion would result in the reference back of' every report made by a committee of this House in order that they might have a second chance. It is precisely the reverse of the principle upon which Sir Wilfrid Laurier acted. Sir Wilfrid Laurier always took firm' ground that when any matter had been referred to a committee of the House and had been dealt with by that committee and opportunity had been given for the consideration of every question so referred, the report of the committee ought to be adopted and approved by the House unless the strongest possible reasons to the contrary could be substantiated. I think that is a very good principle in any case, but particularly I think it is a good principle to apply to the report of a committee which has been so active, so earnest and so zealous in its work as the committee in ' question.
I would like to emphasize what has been said by one or two hon. members. It is perfectly easy for us, sitting in this Chamber, to vote that a great many millions shall be provided for the purpose of making loans, but it is an entirely different question when you come to look around for the money with which to do it. I sometimes doubt whether hon. members realize just what the financial burdens of this country are. Twenty-four years ago to-morrow I was first elected to this House. When I came here in 1896 one usual ground of contention between the parties during the previous three, four or five years, and one serious ground of contention then, was whether or not the expenditure ought to be above or below $40,000,000 in each year. The interest on the public debt to-day is $100,000,000 more than the amount which was regarded as a reasonable annual public expenditure twenty-four years ago. The pension list of Canada has increased-it is very properly increased by the committee to whom the question was referred-until it is almost equal to the total expenditure of this country when I first entered Parliament. I think we must all realize, earnest as we are in the desire to help in every way the men who have done so splendidly their duty at the front, that there is, nevertheless, a Teal limit beyond which we cannot
go in the provision of money, whether by grant or loan or other method, and I hope that the House will bear that in mind. The member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) has put his case very forcibly to the House and he has been eloquently supported by my hon. friend from Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon). The hon. gentleman's motion, in the terms in which it was proposed, does not quite express what he had in mind. It reads as follows:
That the said report be not now concurred in, but that it he recommitted to the Special Committee appointed to consider the continuance of the war bonus, with instructions that they have power to amend the same so as to recommend that subsidies he granted to fishermen as well as farmers.
My hon. friend explains that the intent of his amendment is to provide something in the form of loans, and we shall accept, of course, the meaning which he had in mind. But may I point out to my hon. friend from Skeena, my hon. friend from Gloucester and other gentlemen who have spoken in this matter that as soon as the report of this committee was made and presented to the House, the Government felt so impressed by that, reporthaving regard to the personnel of the committee, and the work which to the knowledge of the Government that committee had done, and the devotion and ability which they had brought to the task-that we immediately placed on the Ordets of the Day the resolutions necessary to carry out that which the committee had recommended. We subtracted nothing; we took the report of the committee as a whole and put on the Order Paper the resolutions necessary to carry it out. I had hoped to make some progress with these resolutions this afternoon., and I trust that before the House rises to-night we shall make some progress and have the Bills introduced and read the first time. But if the motion of my hon. friend from Skeena should prevail and this report should be referred back, what would be the position of the Government? Are we to hold our hand and take no further action until we know whether or not that report is to be modified? That must Tesult in one of two things: either prorogation will have to be deferred for some time, or we shall let this legislation stand over until another session. I am anxious, .and I know that my hon. friend from Skeena is anxious, to give effect to the report of the committee in so far as it does bring aid and comfort and help to those who have fought for us in the war and to their dependent's. Now, if this report is referred back, the committee will either go through the empty form of
395$

having another vote or it must embark once more upon a careful examination of the matters to which they have already given attention during some nine. weeks. Under the circumstances, is it possible for ug to imagine that the one course or the other would really result in inducing members of the committee to alter the opinion which they have already expressed? I hope, therefore, that the hon. member for Skeena and the hon. member for Gloucester, whose views in these matters are entitled to the utmost respect, will see the advantage, from the standpoint of the returned men themselves of having the aid and comfort and help recommended by the committee embodied in actual legislative proposals and passed by Parliament at the present session. That is what the Government had in mind; that was the impelling reason that induced the Government, the very moment this report was laid on the table of the House, to place upon the Order Paper the resolutions necessary to carry it out.
I do not know whether under the rules of debate I am entitled to reply.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: No, the hon. member (Mr. Peck) is not entitled to Teply, but if he desires to ask the unanimous consent of the House to do so, I will submit the question to the House. I? it the pleasure of the House that the hon. member have leave to reply?
Carried.

Before the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) replies, I may say that if the question is going to a vote I wish to make a few remarks. If, on the other hand, the hon. member intends to withdraw his amendment, I do not care to take up the time of the House. If my hon. friend is not going to withdraw his amendment-
I am in a very difficult situation-	.
-I will say just a word or two. It will take me only a few moments.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not understood that the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Peck) now closes the debate.
All right.

I am put in a most difficult situation. The reason I moved this amendment was because I wanted to achieve results, and I thought that my amendment in regard to fishermen had the beet chance of carrying of anything that might be suggested in regard to the re-establishment of 
returned soldiers. Many other suggestions in that direction might be made, but I did not. consider that they had the same prospect of carrying. When hon. gentlemen eay to me "The fishermen are a class;'' I know that quite well, and I pointed out in my speech that that argument would be used, and it has been used by hon. gentlemen who professed to be great opponents of what they are pleased to call legislation for a class. The Prime Minister Sir Robert Borden), if I understand him aright, says to this House that the effect of adopting my amendment would be to put the House in the position of showing a callous indifference to the report of the committee or to delay prorogation. If that be the case, I certainly will not stand in the way, as I said in the earlier part of my speech, of all the good things, that may be done for returned soldiers and their dependents in accordance with the report of the committee. If we are to accept the statement that this report must go through in its present form or not at all, I am going to withdraw my amendment, but I would appeal to the Government and to the House to do something for the returned soldier in the direction I have indicated. I do not care about technical forms or what you do with them. Men say that you should not act in this manner because this, because that, or because the other thing, as regards the committee report. But what I want to achieve is results, and if the Government promises and if the House will do better things than my poor amendment will achieve, I am prepared to withdraw my amendment. All I want to do is to get the very most I can for the returned soldier, and I took this question of aid to the fishermen, which I knew so many members on both sides have stated they are in favour of, as the one thing that was most likely to pass in the House. I am prepared to accept what the right hon. gentleman who leads the House may give us and what I think we may get, and with the consent of the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Tur-geon), I will withdraw my amendment.

I will assent to that. Amendment withdrawn.
Mr. HUME CRONYN l(London):	Mr. Speaker, may I say just a word-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has the right to reply, but if he speaks now the debate will be closed.

I will not detain ihe
House more than one moment, and I am

not going to cover the ground already so fully covered; but I perceive for the iirst time a communication read by the hon. member for Cape Breton North and Victoria (Mr. McKenzie), and I think it is only due to this House and to the gentlemen concerned that I should make some explanation in regard to the matter. It is quite true that those gentlemen did communicate with the .committee and requested to be called and to present, as well, a statement of their contentions or recommendations. They were not called, and the reason why they were not called was that the committee found Parliament nearing prorogation and, therefore, was quite unable to hear a good deal of the evidence which was to have been tendered to it. The committee itself decided that those gentlemen should not be called. Complaint is made that I am discourteous in not replying to a letter which those gentlemen addressed to me. The facte are that those gentlemen, being in Ottawa for some other purpose, saw the clerk of the committee, and, as I am told, he had explained to them the reason why their evidence could not be heard. They did not see me, the chairman of the committee, nor the vice-chairman, nor, so far as I am aware, any other member of the committee. They sent a letter of protest, and I regret to say that that letter, which reached me, I think, only a few days ago, lay on my desk amongst at least one hundred other unanswered letters. I have not been able to give a moment of time to anything other than the preparation of this report and the laying of it before the House. I regret as much as any one could my failure to answer that letter. The circumstances prevented our hearing those gentlemen; we sat too long, as the hon. member says, and as I thoroughly agree; but we had before us, not only nearly 700 communications, but 500 pages of various suggestions, resolutions and reports from different bodies. We could have sat for another two months and still not have completed our work.
Motion to adopt the report of the committee agreed to.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I beg to move:
That In view of the late period of the session, Private Bills sent by the Senate to this House for concurrence he read twice on the same day, and that Rule 103, relative to the posting of such Bills, be suspended for the remainder of the session.
He said: I am informed that unless this motion passes, a number of Bills in respect of which a great deal of work has been done in the Senate and a good deal of expense incurred as well, will have to be dropped.
I have no recollection of ever before hearing such a motion as that moved by the Prime Minister.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have frequently seen motions of that character which suspend formal rules of the House at a late period of the session.
Motion agreed to.

I move:
That Bill No. 193 (from the Senate) for the relief of Nora Dowle, be placed on the Order Paper amongst Private Bills for second reading this day.

subtopic: RULES OF HOUSE SUSPENDED TO EXPEDITE THE LEGISLATION BASED ON REPORT OF PENSIONS COMMITTEE.

speakeroldname: Rt. Hon. Sir ROBERT BORDEN (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: RULES OF HOUSE SUSPENDED TO EXPEDITE THE LEGISLATION BASED ON REPORT OF PENSIONS COMMITTEE.
speechtext: In view of what I said just now upon the amendment of the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Peck), I would ask the House, if it meets with their approval, to permit such of the resolutions on the Order Paper as are based upon the report of the Committee on Pensions and Reestablishment to be passed in order that the Bills may be introduced and read a first time. Of course, we shall have to go into committee on the resolutions; and I mean simply this, that, under the circumstances, as the report has been approved and as all these Bills are founded upon that report, and, moreover, as all these Bills are in the form recommended by the committee after careful consideration, we might for the purpose of advancing the proceedings a stage, take the resolutions pro forma, as there will still be most ample opportunity of discussing the subject either upon the second reading of the Bills or in committee of the whole House upon the Bills.

subtopic: RULES OF HOUSE SUSPENDED TO EXPEDITE THE LEGISLATION BASED ON REPORT OF PENSIONS COMMITTEE.
speechtext:
I see no
objection to the course my right hon. friend has proposed. I agree that it will expedite the legislation, and it is obviously in the interests of the returned soldiers and the public that we should expedite it.

On the motion of Rt. Hon. Sir Robert Borden (Prime Minister) (for Sir Henry Drayton) the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin the Chair:
Resolved,-1. That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide that the Minister of Finance or such other minister as the Governor in Council may determine may enter into an insurance contract with any returned soldier domiciled or resident in Canada or any widow of a soldier so domiciled or resident for the payment of five hundred dollars or any multiple thereof not exceeding five thousand dollars, one-fifth thereof payable on death of insured and the remainder at option of insured, and after his death at the option of the beneficiary as a life annuity or as an annuity certain for five, ten, fifteen or twenty years, or as an annuity guaranteed for five, ten, fifteen or twenty years and payable thereafter as long as the beneficiary may live.
2.	That the contract may provide that the payment of premiums may be waived if the insured becomes totally disabled, if such disability does not entitle him to a pension under the Pension Act, that he may receive an amount not exceeding one-twentieth of the sum insured but not to exceed twenty payments in all, and that if he dies before such payments are completed the balance assured may be paid as a death benefit.
3.	That the payment be made to the wife, husband, child, grandchild, parent, brother or sister of insured or person entitled under any regulation to be a beneficiary.
4.	That if insured is a married man or a widow with child or children the insurance shall be for their benefit, or some onto or more of them at insured's option: if a widow the insurance shall be for the benefit of such person or persons within the classes mentioned in resolution three as may be shown to the satisfaction of the minister to be to a substantial extent dependent on the widow; if an unmarried man or a widower without children the insurance shall be for his future wife or future wife and children.
5.	That where a beneficiary dies in the life time of the insured he may declare that the share of such person shall be for the benefit of his wife or child or one or more of them, and, in default of such declaration, the share shall be apportioned in equal shares if there is more than one beneficiary. If all beneficiaries so die the insured may declare that the money shall be for the benefit of his wife or his surviving children, if any, and if he makes no declaration the money shall be divided equally among his wife and surviving children, and, if there is no wife or children, the money, subject to the provisions mentioned in resolution three, shall become part of his estate.
6.	That if on the death of the insured a pension becomes payable under The Pension Act to any person or persons within the classes men- , tioned in resolution three there shall be deducted from the benefit payable the aggregate present value of the pension or pensions so payable computed on such basis as may be prescribed by regulation, and in such case there shall be returned to the beneficiary or beneficiaries in proportion to their respective interests under the contract the proportion of the premiums

paid (with interest at four per cent per annum, compounded annually), which the amount of the said deduction is of the total amount assured under the contract.
7.	That if the insured survives all the persons to whom the death benefit may be paid under the provisions of resolution three, or if all the said persons die before the payment of the instalments of the death benefit have been completed, the estate of the insured shall be entitled to receive only thie amount by which the reserve under the contract at the time of the death of the insured exceeds the sum of the payments so made. In this resolution the word " reserve " means the net premium value of the contract on the basis of the British Offices Life Tables, 1893, Om (5), with interest at the rate of four per cent per annum.
8.	That when no apportionment is made of the insurance money all persons interested t« beneficiaries shall share equally therein.
9.	That the contract may provide for payment of a single premium or premiums uniform throughout the lifetime of insured or during lifetime of insured for ten, fifteen, or twenty years, or until the age of sixty-five.
10.	That no medical examination shall be necessary unless the minister deems it necessary to enable him to decide whether or not he will refuse in any particular case to insure.
11.	That the insurance shall not be assignable or liable to claims of creditors.
12.	That the Governor in Council may make regulations respecting forms of contract, proof of age, etc., and for carrying out the purposes of the Act.
13.	That moneys received shall be paid into the Consolidated Revenue Fund, and moneys payable shall be paid out of such fund.
14.	That an annual statement shall be laid before Parliament.
15.	That no contract of insurance shall be entered into after July 1, 1922, and that the measure shall come into force on August 1, 1920.
Resolution reported.
Sir ROBERT BORDEN (for the Minister of Finance) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 195, to provide for the insurance of returned soldiers by the Dominion of Canada.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: ROYAL CANADIAN MOUNTED POLICE ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext:

Resolved, That. it Is expedient to bring in a measure to repeal the proviso to section eight of chapter sixty-nine of the statutes of 1919, which provides that the amount of any pension, gratuity or allowance which any member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police receives or is entitled to receive or apply for, in respect of any injury received by him while serving in the military, naval or air forces aforesaid (that is to say, of His Majesty) shall he deducted from any pension, gratuity or allowance to which

On the motion of Rt. Hon. Sir Robert Borden (Prime Minister) the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Boivin in the Chair:
Resolved, That it is expedient to amend the Pension Act, chapter 43 of the statutes of 1919 and to provide:-
1.	That the salaries of the two commissioners shall be increased from $5,000 to $6,000 per annum.
2.	That the commission shall award pensions to or in respect of members of the force who have suffered disability in accordance with schedule A hereto, and to or in respect of members of the force who have died in accordance with schedule B hereto.
3.	That the provisions of section 12 relating to cases of intemperance or improper conduct, shall not apply when the death of a member of the force has occured on service.
4.	That section 13, relating to the time within which application must be made for pension, be amended to provide that application may be made within three years after the date of the completion of his treatment by the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment when he was retired or discharged direct to such treatment or undertook such treatment within six months after his retirement or discharge.
5.	That section 14 be amended to provide that pensions shall be awarded according to rank or acting rank at the time of appearance of "the injury or disease" instead of "the disability," and that the same amendment do apply to cases of voluntary reversion.
6.	That section 17 relating to suspension of pension on imprisonment be amended to provide that payment may be re-considered upon the pensioner's release in accordance with the extent of his disability then shown to exist.
7.	That section 22 of the said Act relating to persons receiving several pensions be repealed.
8.	That subsection one of section 23 relating to pensions to children be amended to provide that no pension shall be paid to or in respect of a child who, if a boy, is over the age of sixteen years or, if a girl, is over the age of seventeen years, except when such child and those responsible for its maintenance are without resources and,-
(a)	such child is unable owing to physical or mental infirmity to provide for its own maintenance, in which case the pension may be paid while such child is incapacitated by physical or mental infirmity from earning a livelihood provided that no pension shall be awarded unless such infirmity occurred before the child attained the age of twenty-one years; and provided also that if such child is an orphan the commission shall" have discretion to increase such child's pension up to an amount not exceeding orphans' rates:
(b)	such child is following and is making satisfactory progress in a course of instruction approved by the commission, in which case the pension may be paid until such child has attained the age of twenty-one years.
No pension shall be paid to or in respect of a child after its marriage.
And, further, that in subsection two of this section, the term "appearance of the injury or

disease" shall be substituted for the words occurrence or appearance of the disability."
9.	That subsection 3 of section 25, relating to pensions for disabilities, be amended to provide that no pension shall be paid for a disability or disabling condition which at such time was wilfully concealed, was obvious or was a congenital defect.
10.	That subsection 2 of section 26 be amended to provide that whenever a pensioner is required by the commission to be medically reexamined he shall be paid a reasonable amount for travelling expenses, subsistance and loss of wages. If any pensioner, after notice by registered mail, unreasonably refuses or neglects to present himself for medical re-examination, his pension shall be suspended and no pension shall be paid him in respect of the period during which such refusal or neglect continues.
11.	That the provision of subsection 1 of section 27 of an extra alloVance for total disability be amended to provide that the addition to the pension may be not less than $250, and not exceeding $750 per annum.
12.	That subsection 2 of section 27 be amended to provide that if such member of the forces holds the rank of Commander and Captain under three years seniority (Naval) or Lieutenant Colonel (Militia) he shall be entitled to an addition to his pension not exceeding ninety dollars per annum, if he holds the rank of Lieutenant Commander (Naval) or Major (Militia) to an addition to his pension not exceeding three hundred and ninety dollars per annum, and if he holds the rank of Lieutenant (Naval) or Captain (Militia) to an addition to his pension not exceeding six hundred and fifty dollars per annum.
13.	That the provisions of paragraph (b) of section 28, relating to the time from which pension shall be paid, be amended, to provide, that in the case in which a pension is awarded to an applicant the appearance of whose injury or disease which caused his disability was subsequent to his retirement or discharge the pension shall be paid from the day upon which the application for pension has been received.
14.	That section 30 be amended by adding thereto the provision that when a pensioner commences treatment under the jurisdiction of the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment and his pension, including the pension, if any, for his dependents, is greater than the pay and allowances issued by that department, there shall be deducted from such pension towards the cost of maintenance in hospital an amount equal to the difference between such pension and such pay and allowances.
15.	That the provisions of subsection 3 of section 31, relating to the maintenance of parents, be repealed, and in lieu thereof it be enacted that when a member of the forces, previous to his enlistment or during his service, was maintaining or was substantially assisting in maintaining one or both of his parents, an amount not exceeding one hundred and eighty dollars per annum may be paid to him for each of such parents as long as he continues such maintenance.
16.	That section 32 be repealed, and in lieu thereof it be enacted that when a pensioner pensioned on account of a disability has died and his estate is not sufficient to pay the expenses of his last sickness and burial, the Commission may pay such expenses, or a portion thereof, but the payment in any such case shall not exceed one hundred dollars.

17.	That the provision of subsection 1 of section 33 be amended to provide that no pension shall be paid to the widow of a member of the forces unless she was married to him before the appearance of injury or disease which resulted in his death.
18.	That subsection 2 of section 34 be repealed and in lieu thereof it be enacted that in cases in which a member of the forces has died leaving a widow or a widow and children or orphan children entitled to pension in addition to a parent or person in the place of a parent who previous to his enlistment or during his service was wholly or to a substantial extent maintained by him, the Commission may, in its discretion, award a pension to each such parent or person not exceeding one hundred and eighty dollars per annum.
19.	That subsection 4 of section 34 be repealed, and in lieu thereof it be enacted that,-
(a)	In cases in which a member of the forces has died leaving more than one parent or person in the place of a parent who were wholly or to a substantial extent maintained by him, the pension for one such parent or person may be increased by an additional amount not exceeding one hundred and eighty dollars per annum and the total pension apportioned between such parents or between the parent and such other person.
(b)	The pension to any parent or person in the place of a parent shall be subject to review from time to time and shall be continued, increased, decreased or discontinued in accordance with the amount deemed necessary by the Commission to provide a maintenance for such parent or person, but in no case shall such pension exceed the amount of pension prescribed for parents in Schedule B of this Act.
(c)	When a parent or person in the place of a parent has unmarried sons residing with him or her who should, in the opinion of the Commission, be earning an amount sufficient to permit them to contribute to the support of such parent or person, each such unmarried son shall be deemed to be contributing not less than ten dollars a month towards such support.
(d)	The pension to a widowed mother shall not be reduced on account of her earnings from personal employment or on account of her having free lodgings or so long as she resides in Canada on account of her having an income from other sources which does not exceed two hundred and forty dollars per annum.
(e)	The pension to a parent or person in the place of a parent shall not be reduced on account of the payment to such parent or person of municipal insurance on the life of a deceased member of the forces.
20.	That section 38 be repealed, and in lieu thereof it be enacted that pensions awarded with respect to the death of a member of the forces shall be paid from the day following the day of the death except,-
"(a) in the case in which a pension is awarded to a parent who was not wholly or to a substantial extent maintained by the member of the forces at the time of his death, in which case the pension shall be paid from a day to be fixed in each case by the Commission; and
"(b) in the case of a posthumous child of a member of the forces, in which case the pension for such child shall be paid from the date of its birth."
21.	That section 46, relating to supplementary pensions for disability in respect of members

of the Allied Forces other than those of Canada, be amended to make this section applicable only to persons of the rank of Warrant Officer or of a higher rank.
22.	That section 47 he repealed and it be inact-ed in lieu thereof that when a person of the rank of Warrant Officer or of a higher rank in any of His Majesty's naval, military or air forces other than the naval, military or air forces of Canada, or when a person in the naval, military or air forces of one of His Majesty's Allies who was domiciled and resident in Canada at the beginning of the war has died during the war or thereafter as the result of a disability incurred during the war or demobilization and his widowed mother, widow or children have been awarded a smaller pension than they would have been entitled to under this Act in respect of his death, such widowed mother, widow or children shall be entitled, during the continuance of their residence in Canada, to such additional pension as will make the total of the two pensions received by them equal to the pension that would have been awarded if the person aforesaid had died in the military service of Canada."
23.	That the following provisions be added to the said Act:-
"47a. The pensions which are now being paid by Great Britain for disabilities or deaths which occurred during the South African war to or in respect of members of the Canadian Contingents which served in that war shall hereafter be supplemented during the continuance of the residence in Canada of the recipients of such pensions by such additional pensions as will make the total of the two pensions received by them equal to the pension that would have been awarded if they had been disabled or had died in the military service of Canada during the war.
"47b. The pensions which are now being paid to or in respect of members of those forces who served in the Fenian Raid or Northwest Rebellion, during the continuance of the residence in Canada of the recipients of such pensions, shall hereafter be increased to the rates set forth in Schedules A and B to this Act."
24.	That Schedules A and B of the said Act be repealed and the Schedules A and B to these Resolutions be substituted therefor.
25.	That all cases affected by the proposed Act shall be reviewed and future payments shall be made at the rates and in accordance with the provisions set forth herein. Provided that when death or disability has occurred previous to the coming into force of the proposed Act, the provisions of the Act shall not operate to remove from any applicant for pension any rights which he had in virtue of the Pension Act.
26.	That the Act to be based upon these Resolutions shall come into force on the first day of September, 1920.
