Article 18 of the League of Nations provides:
Tout traits ou engagement international con-clu a l'avenir par un membre de la sociStS de-vra etre immSdiatement enregistrS par le Secretariat et publiS par lui aussitOt qu possible. Aucun de ees traitSs ou engagements interna-tionaux ne sera obligatoire avant d'avoir StS enregistrS.
Do commercial treaties as well as purely political treaties come under this article?

I am afraid that in this instance I can only quote what the hon. member has already quoted. As we understand it, every treaty entered into after the signing of the pact by any member of the League with a non-member, or by members of the League with each other, must be registered with a department that is part of the Secretariat of the League. That department examines the Treaty, and if it contains anything contrary to the spirit or the letter of the Covenant, the treaty is not accepted and the nation is asked to revise it. It is hoped and expected that in that way open diplomacy will be encouraged, and that no engagement will be made that might involve nations in war in support of one another. The department has only just been set up. As I understand it, every nation is bound to register its treaty, and any nation that refused would by that very act render itself no longer a member of the League.
Of understand, then, that all treaties are to be subject to the approval of the Assembly of the Council of the League?

All treaties.
Mr. iBELAND: The hon. member referred to the public and private sittings of the Council during the last five months. I did not quite understand in what particulars the two kinds of sittings differed. Will the hon. gentleman give us some information regarding the difference?

The sessions of
the Council of the League of Nations usually take place about a month apart. From four to eight days are devoted to a session. Generally they sit perhaps one or two days in secret session, and then they hold a public session. The votes are always taken at a public session. At this session the rapporteur presents the resolution that has been agreed upon and makes a statement in support of it. Usually the public sessions are social functions, there being generally present several ambassadors and a certain
number of the public-in fact, any one who desires to be present can attend so far as the limited space will allow. Generally fifty or sixty newspaper men are present to report all the details that are given. The private meetings are of a more or less informal character, and they are considered to be absolutely necessary in order that there may be the utmost freedom of discussion among the representatives. I have been able to attend several private meetings when I presented my budget, or where there has been discussion on some matter that required financing, and I have been struck, as I said in my speech, with the determination to always artive at a unanimous agreement. I have seen a question brought up that developed a very considerable difference of opinion, I have seen it discussed for an hour and then withdrawn, the Chairman saying, "Gentlemen, you have had an opportunity of hearing all the different points of view. We will take this question up again the day after tomorrow." When the question came up again it would be considerably amended, and in its amended form it would show evidence of an attempt to meet the different points of view. Perhaps that question would come up at three or four successive meetings until finally it was presented in such shape that it would be passed unanimously, and then action wcjuld follow.

Is there a time limit
within which treaties secretly made must be registered?
As I understand it, no treaty is valid until it is registered; that is, no nation which is a member of the League is bound to observe the treaty.
If a nation on failure to register a treaty is thereby ipso facto outside the League, it seems to me that that is an easy way to dissolve the League.
The nation that has refused to do what it contracted to do would be expected to withdraw from the League.

If secret treaties were
entered into by powerful nations, and those nations refused to register the treaties, on discovery of their failure to so register the League is dissolved.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That would not dissolve
the League of Nations.
If the Great Powers went out of the League where would you get the force to keep it alive.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The nation that violated the provisions of the Covenant would be expelled from the League, but it does not cease to be a member by simply failing to comply with the terms of the League.
After expulsion?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The League would have to take action to expel any offending members.
And after expulsion they are no longer members?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

Therefore if the Great
Nations withdrew the League would be dissolved?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
That is the point.

My hon. friend referred
to the unanimity which always prevailed at the meetings which he attended, and which is bound to prevail in all the decisions reached by the Council of Nine. I also understood him to say that if the representative of Canada were invited to sit at the Council of Nine, not as one of the Nine, he would have the right to express an opinion and to register a vote on a decision. Some doubt has been expressed in this House o.n more than one occasion whether the member of the Assembly of the League of Nations who is invited to sit in the Council of Nine has the right to vote when a question affecting his country is under consideration.

As I understand it, if it was a question in which Canada was vitally interested, and Canada was invited to have her representatives sit at the table for the discussion of the question, Canada's vote cast against the decision would prevent its ratification. A short time ago we had a discussion relating to Poland. The Polish delegates were invited to sit at the Council table. As I understand it, if a decision had been arrived at to which the Polish delegates objected, that decision would not have been persisted in.

We will take it for granted that what the hon. member states is correct. His opinion is of weight in the 'matter, though no clause in the covenant justifies the categorical expression of that opinion. The hon. member has referred also the action taken with regard to the Saar Basin. He did not, however, find it opportune this evening to tell the House what particular

arrangement had been made with regard to the Saar Basin.

I am not sure
that I understand the hon. member's question. If he wants to know what position the Canadian member of the Council occupies and what work he has been especially identified with
Not at all; I know that very well. WThat decision has been reached regarding the future of the Saar Basin and the population in that district?

No decision on that matter has as yet been arrived at. The understanding is that for fifteen years the Saar Basin will be governed by the League of Nations, presumably through the Commission which is at present operating. At the end of the fifteen years a decision will be reached whether the Saar Basin will become part of Germany, part of France, or an independent state.
That ie the political side of it, but what about the economic side,- the coal mines, for instance, to which the hon. member has referred?

That is all set forth in the Treaty. I can give the hon. member, if he desires to study it, a copy of all the special regulations that relate to the Saar Basin as extracted from the Treaty and as interpreted by the various regulations, and reports that the Commission has made during the past three months. It is all laid down in the Treaty; it is quite voluminous.

But can the hon. gentleman tell the committee in a few words whether these mines are going to be exploited for the profit of France exclusively, or for the profit of Germany? I believe that France has retained the power to exploit those mines.

ll think I can only tell the hon. member that that is all set forth in the Treaty. A commission of five members to administer the Saar Basin was appointed at the first and second meetings of the Council of the League of Nations. For the time being they have very wide powers in the Saar Basin. They administer practically all the affairs of that district; the civil service, railways, telephones and telegraphs are all under their control. It is their duty to see that the stipulations in the Treaty with respect to the coal and the proportion of it which will reach France

shall be strictly adhered to. Under their guidance I think they are adhered to.
Will the hon. member explain how the League of Nations proposes to enforce its decisions?
Will my hon. friend be a little more specific? Give me a specific instance.
The League of Nations arrives at certain decisions. Horw does it propose to enforce those decisions?

Possibly the hon. member has in mind a subject that was dealt with at the sixth meeting otf the League of Nations, namely, help to Persia. Persia has been invaded by the Russians. Persia has apealed to the League of Nations. The League of Nations found that Persia was negotiating (with the Bolsheviks at the time for terms of peace. While awaiting the reply from Moscow it was impossible for the League to take on definite responsibility, but at its meeting the Council notified Persia that if the attack was persisted in the League would stand behind Persia. Now, as to the method by which it is done let me give an illustration. In New York city you have a fire brigade and you have a municipal service that taxes the people and pays for that fire brigade. But there are fire stations scattered all over New York city from the Battery to the Bronx. If a fire should break out at the Battery they would not send the engines from the Bronx to put it out; they would send the engines that were nearest to where the fire originated. But the expense would fall upon the whole of the citizens of New York city because the expense of the fire brigade is paid by the citizens as a whole. If it becomes necessary in the defence of members of the League of Nations that various sister nations come to the rescue of a nation which is unjustly attacked, naturally the forces used will be the forces nearest the spot; but when it becomes necessary to determine how much the expedition cost the expense will be levied proportionately on all members of the League.
Who is going to put this machinery in motion and to decide which is the nearest nation?
The Council of the League of Nations will be called. In a case of that kind an emergency meeting can be called within six days, and the machinery could be immediately put into motion.

The hon. member has laid stress upon the judicial functions of the League of Nations. Now, the very essence of judicial function is that the judges shall have no interest whatever in the suit or matter laid before them for decision. How, therefore, do you carry out the parallel, when the nations concerned have, perhaps, very much of a private national interest in the matter to be determined?
I think it is understood that whenever a question comes up for decision in which two members of the League of Nations are interested, they shall both abstain from voting.

Returning to this question otf Persia, I may point out that there is no analogy between the case of the fire department and that of calling upon certain nations to act as suggested, because people do not get killed in putting out a fire but they do when they go to war. What guarantee is there that the Italians, if called upon, as the nearest people, to take action, would do so? Is that agreed to?

Well, you have to take it for granted that the nations who have signed and subscribed to the covenant of the League of Nations will live up to their obligations. I do not think we can quite discuss what would happen if a nation, having, signed the covenant, should refuse to fulfil it. The understanding is that the Council of the League of Nations can take such steps as are necessary for the defence of any nation that is unjustly attacked.
As a member of the League of Nations, we ourselves are under some obligation to respond to a demand of the League of Nations for an armed force?
Yes.
To what extent would we be called upon to contribute an armed force if we happened to find ourselves near the place where, the trouble was?
Such as the United States, for example?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The situation as already explained by my hon. friend (Sir Herbert Ames) is this; that in case a dispute should arise and the Council of the League should decide that armed forces should be called upon to assist in settling that dispute, they would have to summon to the Council the nations which they considered should pro-



vide the armed forces; the representatives of those nations "would be entitled to sit on the Council for the purpose of considering and determining that matter, and no country could be called upon to contribute an armed force unless its representative on the Council agreed that that nation should contribute that force. There can be no compulsion. It has been pointed out to this House before that the success of the League depends upon the co-operation and goodwill of the nations who are parties to it, backed by the sound moral sense and public opinion of the world. The League of Nations, in the last analysis, depends upon the public opinion of the world for its justification and support.

Supposing the nation in closest proximity to the seat of trouble, on being called upon to act, after having a representative on the Council, refuses to act and the next-nearest nation was called upon and it refuses to act, how far back will the matter be carried until somebody does act?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: If this nation or any other nation were to accept the advice of the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and disarm, that nation would at once put itself into a position of being unable to obey the request of the League of Nations if it "were called upon to police some other locality? Is that not so?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I do not know that it
would be profitable for us to enter on a review of the question of disarmament on a discussion of this item, I think we had better confine ourselves to the matter under discussion. The hon. member is, however, quite correct. The League of Nations contemplates the existence of force in the nations that are parties to the Treaty and the use of that force for the purpose of preserving the world peace as against a nation which violates its obligations under the Treaty or is disturbing the peace of the world. It does not aim at the complete elimination of armaments; it does aim at a substantial reduction in armaments, in reducing armaments proportionately to a much more moderate basis than that which exists in Europe to-day, although no suggestion has been made to any nation in Eurpoe of a reduction in armanments that could compare with the maximum that is proposed in Canada.

I should not like to be understood as opposing a genuine, reasonable and well-thought-out attempt to bring about the cessation or diminution of war, and I was struck with one sentence that fell from the lips of my hon. friend (Sir Robert Ames), when he said that, amongst other things, the League of Nations would undertake the study of the causes of war and the removal of those causes. If the League of Nations does nothing but that, it will be taking a long step towards the diminution of war. The study of the causes and the scientific and intelligent removal of the causes of war are

the first steps. To begin this attempt at the diminution of war, to precede all discussion by disarmament is, in my judgment, the height of nonsense. I can never subscribe to that, but I agree that the League of Nations can do a very useful work, in the first place, by studying the causes of war and, in the second place, by attempting to remove those causes.

The hon. member need have no anxiety that disarmament will come suddenly to the world. All the tendency is the other way. But I think he will admit that what has already been done to that ultimate end is wise. When the meeting of the Council was held in Rome, there were present representatives of the armies, navies and air forces of nearly all the principal nations. A committee of twenty-seven was, or is being formed, there being nine naval, nine air and nine military experts on this committee. Their duties are both immediate and future, their immediate duties being to examine carefully into the military strength of each nation which applies for admission to the League with a view to seeing whether these nations are likely to be militaristic in character and to set the extent of the military strength that one of these new nations entering the League may be permitted to carry. Their second duty is to prepare a convention with a view to securing the recording of all sales of arms that are made by nations in Europe to undeveloped peoples in other parts of the world. It is realized that there is an immense stock of ammunition and arms in the hands of certain nations in Europe who need the money and do not need the arms, and there is a great temptation to them to sell these arms and ammunition to backward countries in other parts of the world. When these backward countries find themselves in possession of modern arms, it is a direct incentive to war. Consequently, the second task that falls upon this expert committee that is now well on in the process of formation is to prepare a scheme by which all such sales of arms must be registered, and no sale of arms can be made without the permission of the League. It is recognized that anything like proportional disarmament is a matter requiring long and careful consideration, but it is expected that this expert committee- which, mind you, is primarily composed of military, naval, and air men,-will first undertake a complete stock-taking, so to speak, of the war possibilities of all the 2524
nations of the world. When the actual facts are obtained, and are codified so that they can be studied, then it will be possible by agreement, I believe, to have a proportional disarmament of the world undertaken, so that no nation will suddenly find itself entirely at the mercy of its neighbour, and that each nation will gradually find that the burden of preparedness which it has hitherto carried can be lessened, knowing that the other nations of the world are doing the same thing. If we can once get the armaments of the world down to such a small extent that no nation can suddenly take any other nation by the throat we shall have gone a long way towards securing everlasting peace.

We have now reached the point where we are asked to believe that the maintenance of peace and the curtailment of armaments are the aims of the League of Nations, and also, we are told, of the Canadian Government and of the division of St. Antoine, Montreal. I would ask the hon. member if the United States was represented at the meetings of the Council that have been held in the last five months,-the United States being one of the five Great Powers?

I think I can say that no important step has been taken by the Council of the League of Nations since its formation without an opportunity having been afforded to the United States to cooperate. That will be shown by our records. If the United States declined to co-operate, they will never be in a position to say they were not invited to do so on each important matter. As yet they do not officially cooperate. They have on several occasions unofficially permitted prominent Americans to give us the benefit of their views and advice, but so long as the United States is not a member of the League of Nations, it is, of course, not bound by the decisions that are arrived at, nor does it assume any official responsibility for the carrying out of those decisions.
May I ask further whether the hon. member has any information regarding the date of the next convening of the Assembly of the League of Nations, and the place where it will assemble?

At the meeting in Rome it was decided that there shall be a meeting of the Assembly before the end of the present calendar year, and a decision was recorded that this meeting should commence in the first half of No-

vember. The Covenant provides that the first meeting of the Assembly must he called by President Wilson. He was therefore communicated with, and asked to issue the official call. It was suggested to him that one of the capitals of Europe would be a proper place. Whether Brussels was distinctly stated in the telegram or not I do not remember, but the understanding was that the preference of the Council for the first meeting of the Assembly was for Brussels.
Have Belgium, Spain, Greece and Brazil been represented at the different meetings of the Council?

Every meeting of *the Council has been attended by eight members. They are not always the same persons, although, generally speaking, the representation is continuous. The four principal Powers, and Belgium, Spain, Greece and Brazil are represented at every meeting. The Council has never sat with less nor more than eight members.

President Wilson was designated as the person to call the first meeting, I understand. The United States not being in the League and no one haying been designated to call the second meeting, who will call it?	,
I should presume that the second meeting will take place where the first meeting decides it shall meet.
On adjournment?

Is it the
intention of the League to take any direct action in case of conflicts between Powers?

I	understood
that we had been rather dealing with that question in the case of Persia.

To what
extent is it proposed to limit armaments, if it is the intention of the League to take direct action in such cases?

Although it has always been understood that large standing armies and navies would be reduced, it was never thought there would be a time when there would not be a sufficient army and navy for the polipe purposes of the world.

Why is the
League not taking any action in the matter of the war between Russia and Poland, and the war between Poland and Ukra-nia?

Neither Russia
nor Ukrania is a member of the League. So far as Poland is concerned, Poland's allegation is that this it not a new war, but simply a continuation of their war of self-defence.
Why is not the League taking direct action and settling the difficulties among these nations on the principles which have been enunciated by the hon. member this evening?

The League of
Nations is not setting up the old wars. The League of Nations has to accept the world, when peace is made, and deal with it from then onwards. That brings up this very important difference between the Supreme Council and the League of Nations. We are often asked why the Supreme Council does not bring its duties to an end and make room for the League of Nations. That arises from a misconception of the difference ,between the two bodies. The Supreme Council differs, both in its composition, and in the work that it does, from the League of Nations. The Supreme Council will continue until the Treaties have all been drawn up and accepted, and until the force to cause them to be accepted has been used, if necessary. When the world is at peace it is not expected that there will be very much left for the Supreme Council to do. On the other hand the League of Nations is not merely a small sub-committee of the victorious powers. The League of Nations includes thirteen neutral powers; its powers are curative and constructive and it takes hold where the Supreme Council lets go.
Is it the intention of the League) to recognize, the principle of self-determination, .and if so why does it not recognize the demand of Ukrainia for self-determination?

A state can be
taken into the League as a nation only by the Assembly. Ukrainia is one of eight or ten smaller powers, I understand, that are applying for .admission to the League. If, when the Assembly meets next November, they are satisfied1 that there is a stable government in Ukrainia, that she can be recognized as .an independent nation and that she is prepared to fulfil the obligations that fall upon a League member, the Assembly may then take Ukrainia into the League. They'cannot be taken in except by the Assembly; the Council has not power to do it.

Mr. GRIE.SBACH: The hon. member used the expression,, "recognizing a . nation/' some time ago and said that the League of Nations was not a super-state. Would the League of Nations recognize the belligerency of a revolting country or the independence of a country that had achieved its independence before the Great Powers, or only after it had been recognized either ,as a belligerent or as an independent by the Great Powers?
I do not think that question has ever been raised. The understanding is that each nation makes its application and each nation is considered on its merits.
What is the position of Armenia to-day in relation to mandatory control by the League of Nations?

With respect to Armenia, the first 'Step that is to be taken is to delimit its boundaries. At the present time "Armenia" is a term which spreads over a larger or smaller portion of the map. President Wilson has been asked by the League of Nations to delimit Armenia. That, as I say, is the first step. It still remains to the Supreme Council after these limits are suggested to determine whether they are satisfactory and to take the necessary steps to crystallize that area into a state. Then it becomes necessary to get a mandatory appointed. It has already been suggested that the United States should accept the mandate. The United States, I understand-, has 'declined to do so and therefore it comes back to the Supreme Council to determine what to do with Armenia. The Supreme Council in turn is suggesting to the League of Nations that it should find a mandatory. It is possible that the League of Nations may decide to guarantee a loan of the necessary funds to put Armenia on a sound financial basis and may also guarantee the necessary force to be raised among the powers for its defence, in which case it may be possible to secure some small state that can take over the administration with a feeling that the whole expense will not fall upon them and that they will' not be compelled to maintain a large army in Armenia for its protection.

Has Greece not been
asked to become the mandatory?

I do not think
Greece has been asked to become the mandatory; at least it had not up to the time when I left London.

Mr. Chairman, I
desire to congratulate the hon. member (Sir Herbert Ames) upon the splendid address which he has given us to-night. I have long looked upon him as one of the best types of Christian statesmanship that we have produced in Canada. I have been closely associated with him for about sixteen years and I must say that as a gentleman I hold him in the highest esteem. I have followed with great interest the remarks he has made to-night and I believe that if anybody can make a success of what is a very difficult proposition the hon. gentleman will be able to do his full share.
I am pleased and delighted with the description he has given of the aims and objects of the League. But, as we cannot spend all out time on ideals, he will perhaps pardon me if I draw attention to two1 or three matters in connection with the League of Nations that have been stumbling blocks to myself and in regard to which I have expressed my views in this House on previous occasions.	[DOT]
This is probably the greatest ideal the world has produced up to date. Unless it is the great success that it is expected to be it may prove one of the greatest fallacies the world has ever seen along the line of the attempted control of nations. Just looking at the practical side I want to make a very few remarks. The hon. member for St. Antoine devoted a large part of his remarks to the question of disarmament, and the word "armament" was not mentioned in a way to suggest that armaments were being increased. I do not know that we would be justified, as the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) apparently thought, in cutting down the very meagre Estimates that have been presented to this House for the naval, military and air services. I do not think that the hon, member for St. Antoine himself desired that his speech should be used in that direction. Therefore the leader of the Opposition, who has retired from the Chamber, for the moment, was not justified in seizing upon his remarks at the very earliest opportunity and using them as an argument against the very moderate proposals we are trying to get through the House in the way of naval and military Estimates .
What I would like to have heard from the hon. gentleman who has delivered this .splendid address to-night is a little more about the difficulties that are in the way of the success of the League and- not quite so much about the idealistic period that is expected to arrive in the history of the

I would like
to ask wThat the Budget of the League was during its organizing period, and the amount of Canada's share? I would also like an estimate, if possible, of probable future expenditure.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: Is that the disadvantage of being too big?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes. Canada is one of the contributors, in the higset class; so is Australia; so is England. Under the convention relating t'o the International Postal Union at least five units of the British Empire are in the first class, and on the existing basis we are called upon to contribute more than our real share' having regard to our relative standing with the other nations. I understand that one of the matters to come before the Assembly at its first meeting is a reconsideration of the basis of contribution, with a view to an amendment of the Covenant which will make the basis more equitable. When that basis is agreed upon-our share or contribution will undoubtedly be substantially reduced.	/	t

How does our share compare with the share Great Britain pays?
Mr. ROWEiLL: It is exactly the same as Great Britain's share and the United States' share; Australia's share is the same. I do not know why Canada is on the same basis as Great Britain and the United States in the International Postal Union, but she is, and therefore we are paying now on this basis a larger share than we will after the readjustment is made.
Is the United States paying?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: She is not a member of the League. Of course, if she comes in she will have to pay.
Would our payment be reduced by the entrance of the United States?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
We are paying more now because of the fact that the United States is not in the League?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: All nations which have joined the League are paying more than they would pay if the other nations were also members.
What Canadians are participating in the work of this League?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: In addition to Sir Herbert Ames, who is the financial director, Doctor Riddell, who was Deputy Minister of Labour for the province of Ontario, has recently been appointed in connection with the International Labour Office. I am not quite sure of his exact position but Sir Herbert Ames will be able to tell us. Mr. Waugh has been appointed to the Saar Valley Basin Commission. Those are the three principal appointments.
How many members compose the financial directorate?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Just one.
Mr. MiARCIL (Bonaventure): We have been told that Canada might be represented at the Council of the League if Canadian interests were at stake. Who is to judge when a question affects Canada as distinct from the British Empire; or is Canada called in when a decision may be arrived at in which the Empire alone is represented?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: If the question affected Canada in the sense that Canada might be called upon to take some action under the terms of the Covenant, then Canada would be entitled to be represented at the Council of the League.
Otherwise she has no representation except through the British representative?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Canada is represented
in the assembly in the same way as every other country which is not now represented on the Council.

I see my hon. friend (Sir Herbert Ames) has returned to

his seat. I was asking in his absence what Canadians are participating in the work of the League?

Mr. Waugh, who is on the Saar Valley Basin Governing Commission; Doctor Riddell, who, I understand, came from the Ontario Government, and who occupies a position in the Labour Office in connection with the study of unemployment; there are one or two younger men in subordinate positions and one young lady. Mr. Martel went over, I understand, as the Vice-President of Trades and Labour Council of Montreal. Then to the various committees that are sitting from time to time we send Canadian representatives. At the present moment Mr. Gundy is over there assisting in the organization of the Financial Conference. He came somewhat ahead of time owing to the conference having been postponed, and as he was likely to be in England some time he offered to help the committee, and is doing so I understand.
He made up for the one representative of labour who came after the conference?

Yes. At the present time in Geneva, where a Labour Conference is being held in connection with seamen's working conditions, we have Messrs. Robb, Gauthier and Desbarats. We should be represented at all of these important conferences whenever matters affecting Canada come up for consideration; and I hope that from time to time we may be able to secure outstanding Canadians who will make good as those who have already joined us are doing.
Is it the fact that our Canadian delegates at the Shipping Conference refused to go on until some American delegates were present?
I cannot tell you, because whatever happened there has happened since I returned to Canada.
All these appointments are made on the recommendation of the Canadian Government?

Not necessarily. One of the principles laid down by the League of Nations is that the Secretary-General shall be at liberty to choose men wherever he can find them who have the qualifications, and offer them whatever is necessary to secure their services. Only a short time ago I was deputed to go to Geneva to interview a prom-

inent Swiss gentleman to ascertain whether he would accept an important position in connection with the League of Nations, and I was told to make it very clear to him that if he did not accept the position it would not go to Switzerland, but to a native of Denmark, and that he was invited purely in his personal capacity.

Who is the Secretary-
General?

Sir Eric Drummond, who has had a long experience in external affairs. He was private secretary to Mr. Balfour when the latter visited Canada some years ago, and he was also private Secretary to Lord Grey, when Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs.
What are the probabilities as to the Great Powers which are not now members of the League of Nations entering the League?

It is the earnest desire as far as possible to have every Power great and small enter the League of Nations in due course. For example, I do not think there is any desire to keep out for any prolonged period even those States [DOT]which were originally enemies of the Allies. It is only a question of when the right time arrives for those Powers one by one to be taken in, on condition that they apply to be taken in, and I think practically all of them will apply. In the case of Russia it is impossible to prophesy, because we do not know what condition of affairs exists in that country, nor are we permitted as yet to carry on that inquiry which the League considers to be necessary in order to know the exacst facts regarding the Soviet administration.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Before we pass from this item I wish to mention a matter of some importance in connection with External Affairs. At an earlier period of the session I intimated, in answer to a question put by an hon. member opposite, that if the Hungarian and Turkish Treaties were signed and copies were available in time they would be sumbitted to the House before the House prorogued. Although the Hungarian Treaty has been signed, an authenticated copy has not yet been received; it is, therefore, not possible to submit it to the House this session. The Turkish Treaty has been submitted to the Turkish plenipotentiaries, and although its terms are settled the Turkish plenipotentiaries have not yet made their answer; therefore it will not be possible to submit that Treaty to the House
during the present session. As the principles embodied in these Treaties, however, are similar to those embodied in the Treaties which have already been submitted to and approved by the House, I take it that in the absence of any expression of opinion to the contrary by the House the Government would not be justified in withholding its approval of ratification of these Treaties until another session of Parliament if it should appear to be in the public interest that they should be ratified and put into operation before the House reassembles. I wanted to mention that fact so that the House would be apprised of the situation. If hon. members wish to know anything of the Treaties as submitted, I shall be glad to give them the information.

Can my hon.
friend suggest to the committee any particular injury the world's affairs are likely to suffer through failure on the part of Parliament to ratify these Treaties, and wherein it may be necessary for the Governor in Council to act in order to save the international situation?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I can only repeat what
I have previously said on one or two occasions: that the British Empire cannot ratify these Treaties or put them into effect without the consent of the Government of Canada, one of the constituent nations of the Empire. These Treaties will not be ratified or put into effect unless the British Empire is a party to such ratification.

Does my hon. friend suggest that the Government of Great Britain is prevented from becoming a party to these Treaties with Hungary and Turkey if this Parliament does not take some action in the matter?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, I did not suggest
that. I say that the British Empire will not ratify any of these Treaties without the consent of Canada. It is not Great Britain, but His Majesty, representing the whole Empire, who is a party to the Treaty, and His Majesty will not ratify these Treaties unless all the constituent nations of the Empire approve of the ratification. That Act is an Act of the Government, not of the Parliament of Canada. I intimated that if the copies of the Treaties arrived in time they would be submitted to Parliament so that the Government might have as a basis for its action in recommending ratification the approval of the House as it had in the case of the other Treaties. I now point out that

for the reasons which I have given the Hungarian and Turkish Treaties cannot be submitted to the House during the present session.

Would His
Majesty not have power to ratify on behalf of such parts of the Empire as had expressed their approval? Is it necessary that all should ratify at the same time?
Mr. ROW'ELL:	It may be that His
Majesty could ratify with respect to certain portions of the British Empire; I do not care to enter into a discussion of that question to-night. But His Majesty is not a party as representing a section of the British Empire; he is a party as representing the whole Empire. Up to date all the nations which compose the Empire have acted in concert in ratification and it is hoped they will act in concert in the future.
- \

I trust that the Government will move in the direction of seeing to it that unanimous concurrence shall not be required in order that a Treaty may become effective. I can imagine a case where a Treaty might remain unratified for a considerable time through one of the legislatures, say that of New Zealand, not sitting. In such a case it would seem to be a matter of convenience that the King as representing say, Canada, Australia, South Africa and Great Britain, should be able to ratify so far as these parts of the Empire were concerned, while New Zealand might ratify afterwards.

I should like to say one word to my hon. friend, inasmuch as he has specifically raised this question. The outstanding feature of the address which we heard this evening was the intimation respecting the passing away of the era of secret diplomacy. The note that was sounded most strongly in the House at the beginning of this session was that in these international affairs, certainly in our diplomatic affairs, there should be an end to secrecy and also an end to action by the Governor in Council as a substitute for Parliament. If these Treaties are of any significance at all they ought to be submitted to Parliament; the princip^ of the supremacy of Parliament should be maintained at all costs.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is the reason why
I explained to my hon. friend the situation as it stands. If any hon. member wishes to know the terms of these Treaties we shall be glad to explain them, because we have 
the contents of the Treaties although we have not received the executed documents.

I understand that Anatolia has been handed over to Greece. This question, I believe, has been dealt with by the Turkish Treaty-the question of Anatolia and Smyrna. What is going to happen to these territories?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Under the proposed
Treaty with Turkey, Smyrna and the adjacent territory is under the administrative jurisdiction of Greece, although the sovereignty of Turkey is (preserved over it for a period of five years. At the end of five years a vote is to be taken to determine whether it is to fall under the sovereignty of Greece or to remain under the sovereignty of Turkey.

Despatches have recently
appeared in the press to the effect that Greece is to be given a free hand in cleaning up the Turkish nationalists in these regions, in spite of the serious advice tendered to the Prime Ministers by Marshal Foch and Sir William Wilson. Does the Government know anything about that?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I congratulate my hon.
friend upon his familiarity with the despatches which appear from day to day in the. press. We have no information in the matter.
Shall the item carry?

Before the. item carries I think we should have some information with regard to it. We have spent sufficient time in discussing the matter of the League of Nations; we have been at it since eight o'clock, and I think it is about time we got down to business.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The understanding was
that we would not take up the Civil Government items until the application of the classification was placed on the Table. But the difference in the amount of this item over that of last year is very slight, and I think we could dispose of it in two or three minutes. That, however, rests with my hon. friend (Mr. Mackenzie King); if he desires it, I am willing that the item stand.

Possibly it would be better to keep to the understanding that has been made and not to proceed with Civil Government Estimates until there is laid on the table of the House the reclassification that we have been waiting for during the whole of this session.

Will it be possible under this item to discuss the question of our relations with Washington with reference to the newsprint situation?
Item stands.
Allowance to Mr. W. J. Stewart, Chief Hydro-grapher, for services performed under Order in Council of the 19th October, 1912, in relation to questions under consideration by the International Joint Commission, during the year 1919-20, $1,000.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: A similar item was in last year's Estimates.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He is a consulting -engineer who attends all the meeting' of the International Joint Commission and advises the commission on questions that arise.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There is considerable work in connection with this, and many a night I have known him to be working late hours. He may ibe called as a witness to give expert testimony on any international waterway question that comes up.
If we are paying a man, we want to know if he is a capable man and doing good work. It is not enough for the hon. member -to tell us that Mr. Stewart has been out late and that sort of thing.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: He was one of the commissioners on the International Boundary Disputes Commission of which Sir George Gibbons was chairman as well His title is Chief Hy-drographer.

speechtext:
An Order in Council was passed in 1912, appointing him and fixing the remuneration.
Mr. -CAHILL: Does this man draw a salary from any other department of the Government?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As Chief Hy-drographer he draws a salary, I think, from the Naval Department.
ME CAHILL: What salary?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I cannot answer that.
Does he get this salary by Order in pouncil?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Yes.
Was the Civil Service Commission consulted in the matter?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
He was appointed in 1912 and has been acting ever since. As a matter of fact, Mr. Stewart is- in Europe now in connection with international waterways matters. *
Amount required to meet expenses of the Bake of the Woods Technical Board and the Bake of the Woods Control Board, $10,000.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: This is an item in connection with an award made a couple of ye-ars ago by the International Joint Commission in reference to the Lake of the Woods, and pursuant to that award a domestic Board of Control will be appointed to regulate the waters at the boundary there.
How does it happen that we need two boards?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: The Lake of the Woods Technical Board was the board constituted during the reference before the International Commission. Pursuant to the report made by that body, ,it became necessary to have this second body, the Lake of the Woods Control Board, and the Technical Board (will practically cease now.
What is the personnel of each of these two boards?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Under Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
The personnel of the
Lake of the Woods Technical Board consists of practically the leading engineers of the different departments, Mr. C. G. Chapleau, Mr. Ohallies, Mr. -Stewart-and others-about six or seven different members; I have (forgotten the names of the rest. The personnel of the Lake of the Woods Control Board consists of Mr. Stewart as chairman, and two members appointed by Canada and two appointed by the province of Ontario. The dam that controls the whole situation is at Kenora, and from that dam the waters are regulated back. As the province of Ontario is affected by this matter it has asserted its right to representation on the board.

Who are
the members of the International Waterways Commission at present?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I'he International Joint
Commission at present is composed of five

members, one of the American members having died recently. The Canadian members are Mr. Magrath, Sir William Hearst and Mr. Powell, of St John, N. B. The American members are Mr. Gardner and Mr. Clark.
The province of Quebec used to have a representative on that commission on account of the St. Lawrence.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Judge Mignault
used to be a member.

Is it
merely -an accident that Quebec is overlooked?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It may have been an
accident that the province of Ontario was not represented before. It is turn about. Quebec had a representative; now Ontario has one.
Is the real reason not the fact that there was an accident which happened to Sir William Hearst a few months ago and that this place had to be found for him?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That had absolutely
nothing to do with this.
When was he appointed?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Some four or five months ago. I am not sure of the date.
Before or after the Ontario election ?

speechtext: After. He is thoroughly well qualified for the position.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Powell has been
a member of the Commission for some years.
Does not the minister think Montreal is a city of sufficient importance to be represented on a <M>mmission of this kind?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think any city in Canada is entitled to representation on the commission as a city.

As a national port, I mean?
TMr. Rowell.]

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, because the commission does not deal with national ports. It deals wholly with international questions from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The St. Lawrence is one of the -most important, and that happens to be before the commission at the present time,, but no city is entitled as such to representation on the commission. Every section of the country is entitled to fair consideration in choosing representatives on important commissions such as this.

Might I just voice a
protest from the province of Quebec by reason of the fact that there is no man from our province on this board. Ever since the board was formed it has always had a French-speaking member, if I do not mistake. I am the last man in the world to raise questions of race or religion in this House, but it does seem to me representing as we do the province of Quebec, one of the great maritime sections of the country, a province through which flows for such a long part of its course the greatest river of Canada, and from the fact that for so long that race which composes the majority in our province has had a representative on this board'-it does seem to me too bad that this wholesome custom of dividing the positions for honour among the two great races of which this country is composed has been departed' from in this case.

Does not the Prime Minister think that in view of the importance of the port of Montreal, and the 1,000 miles of the St. Lawrence running through the province of Quebec, that the province deserves some representation on that commission?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My hon. friend will remember that the province of Quebec had representation on the commission, first in the person of the k te Hon. T. Chase Gas-grain, and! afterwards in the person of the present Mr. Justice Mignault,. who has been elevated to the Supreme Court of Canada. It happens, just for the moment, that there is no representative from the province of Quebec on the International Joint Commission. I entirely agree that the point of view just presented should always be kept in mind, and that what my hon. friend has urged should be our aim. No one has greater sympathy with what has been expressed8 in that regard than I have.
I move that the committee rise, report progress, and ask leave to sit again this day.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.

speechtext:
On the motion of Sir Henry Drayton (Minister of Finance) the House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution, Mr. Steele in the Chair:
1.	That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide that in any case where a person (hereinafter called the "purchaser") has entered into a contract with a shipbuilder for the building in Canada of a vessel of not less than three thousand tons, and such contract is approved by the Ministers of Finance and Marine and Fisheries, and a sum not less than ten per centum of the price of such vessel is paid by the purchaser to the shipbuilder in cash at the time the contract is entered into, and, if such cash payment is less than twenty per centum of such price, the payment to the shipbuilder of a further sum which with the said cash payment will amount to not less than twenty per centum of such price, no later than six months after such time, and the payment of a further sum not later than nine months after such time, if the previous payments are less than twenty-five per centum of such price, which will be sufficient with the other said payments to amount to at least twenty-five per centum of the total of such price are contracted for and secured to the satisfaction of the Minister of Finance, and the payment of an additional twenty-five per centum of the price is arranged between the purchaser and the shipbuilder, the Governor in Council may authorize the Minister of Finance to endorse on behalf of His Majesty promissory notes drawn by the purchaser in favour of the shipbuilder for the remaining fifty per centum of the price of the said vessel. The Governor in Council shall prescribe the place where such notes shall be paid, the method of discounting them, and the time when such notes are to be paid.
Provided that the first of such notes shall be made payable at a date not less than twenty-one months after the time the contract was entered into, and the last of such notes shall be made payable at a date not later than fifty-seven months after such time.
2.	That a mortgage on the vessel for the full amount of the notes so endorsed by the Minister of Finance, in such form as the Minister of Justice may approve, shall be giv^n to His Majesty, and the said vessel shall be registed in Canada, and the register shall not be transferred, until the amount secured by the mortgage has been fully satisfied and paid.
3.	That until the amount secured by the mortgage is fully satisfied and paid, the vessel shall be insured and kept insured in favour of His Majesty for such amount and against such risks and in such insurance companies as the Minister of Finance may determine.
Provided that if the vessel is being built for an alien, and the provisions above mentioned with respect to mortgaging the vessel cannot conveniently be complied with, such security for the amount of the said promissory notes endorsed by the Minister of Finance shall be furnished by the purchaser as may be approved by the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.
speechtext:
In asking the concurrence of the committee in this resolution it is necessary for me to refer briefly to the situation in which we find ourselves
to-day in the matter of shipbuilding in Canada. We have a large number of shipbuilding yards in this country, seventeen, if I remember rightly, well equiped, and capable of turning out a maximum net tonnage of 250,000 tons a year. Roughly speaking, we have employed in that industry some 25,000 men. That is the figure which is usually used, but I have been trying to get the best possible information on the subject, and I think a nearer figure would be 23,500 men employed in the industry itself. Besides the men engaged in shipbuilding proper, there are a large number of men of necessity engaged in industries which are dependent upon activity in shipbuilding. It is more difficult to determine the exact number of men employed in these other industries, because they are more widespread and so diverse. But again the figure of 25,000 men has been pretty generally accepted. That may be a little too high; I do not know that it is much too high.
This question of aid to shipbuilding is not a new one. It is one that has been more or less forced upon the attention of the Government. For some considerable time insistent demands have been made, in the first instance, that the country should adopt a system of bonusing shipbuilding in this country. These demands were not only fathered by the shipyards, but were very energetically endorsed by the men employed in the shipyards, the Trades and Labour Council, as, well as by returned soldier organizations, because it so happens that very many returned soldiers have found employment and remunerative employment in shipbuilding. The Government, however, has been unable to see its way to recommend to this House any bonus in connection with shipbuilding. Apart altogether from anything that can be urged in favour of or against the bonus system, a bonus would really not solve the difficulty in this case, which is to see that the men employed in shipbuilding have a chance to continue in their employment. The real difficulty is not a difficulty of price, but of credit. It was a difficulty arising out of exchange troubles, and the impossibility on the one hand, of many purchasers, absolutely solvent making full cash payments for their boats,, and the inability on the other hand, of the shipyards to finance the whole con-11 p.m. struction. Further requests have been made. Different contracts, or proposals for different contracts, have been brought from overseas, and the request -has been made that the sums which were voted by this House for the purpose of

extending credit to overseas nations should be applied in connection with shipbuilding. We had a total vote of something over $100,000,000 of credits, but as a matter of fact only some $30,000,000 or $40,000,000 of that-roughly speaking, but I am approximately correct-has been used. The request was that the balance of these votes should bb applied for the purpose of enabling construction to go on. We were unable to see our way to do that, because after all the whole effect of applying credits on that basis would be that to a very large extent the whole risk would be taken by the country. Instead of doing mat the suggestion was made that, notwithstanding the difficulties of exchange, some cash must be supplied by these purchasers and that in addition to their supplying cash the shipbuilder himself would have to look after his own overhead and profits. The proposition which is now before the committee, and embodied in this resolution, is that twenty-five per cent in cash must be paid by the purchaser, that the shipbuilder has to look after twenty-five per cent and that the remaining twenty-five per cent has to be looked after by an issue of notes made by the purchaser and endorsed by the Government but that the Government's endorsa-tion shall be secured by^a first mortgage on the boat.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.
speechtext:
What about the other
twenty-five per cent? [DOT]

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.
speechtext:
Twenty-five per cent is to'be paid by the purchaser in cash, twenty-five per cent is to be looked after by the shipbuilder and that means that he looks after whatever there is of cost over and above seventy-five per cent. But he looks after his own overhead and he certainly looks after his own profit. That leaves fifty per cent and that fifty per cent it is proposed to raise by an issue of notes issued by the purchaser, endorsed by the Government, and secured by a first mortgage which will put the Government in the position of having an absolute first claim on that boat.
There is just one- other difficulty in connection with mortgages, in some foreign countries where perfectly solvent purchasers are to be found but who cannot well make payments by reason of the fact that exchange works so heavily against them, the laws provide that citizens of those countries cannot be owners of vessels unless those vessels are placed on the register of their country. Of course the mortgage to be of any use to us has to be a mortgage on

a boat of Canadian register, and we must maintain Canadian registration in connection .with all boats which we hold for any mortgage claim. In connection with countries of that kind the resolution means that in those cases security to the full extent must be placed in the hands of the country's bankers, the Bank of Montreal, either at their Paris office in France, or at their London office, before any endorsation takes place. As we require a margin of fifty per cent we provide that . the security, in order to be satisfactory, shall be a security of a similar character. What I mean by that is this. One of the great difficulties is in connection with currency payments for these boats. Some of the French banks and companies, which say that they are anxious to get boats here, are certainly solvent and strong but they do not see their way to making the large loss in exchange, and in a case of that kind the security which would be demanded would be security in the currency of the country that would be ample and sufficient, having regard to the margin of the security that we are insisting on in connection with the mortgage to protect the Government's endorsation. The result of it all is . that the country takes this risk but it takes the risk of taking over a 'Canadian boat at fifty cents on the dollar. As against that risk it ensures private shipbuilding being carried on and the continuance of an industry in which some $47,000,000 has been spent and in which a very large number of our best workers are engaged. That is the only risk.
'Besides the different matters that I have already drawn the attention of hon. gentlemen to, I should point out that we are not bound to take any contract. A contract, before being taken must be passed upon by the Department of Marine and the Department of Finance. It must be passed upon by the Department of Marine because the question of the price is an important one and the department is in a position to pass upon that issue; also because the question as to the power of the contracting firm to build a proper boat is a very vital matter and that department again is in a position to determine that point. It must be passed upon by the Finance Department because the question of the solvency of the purchaser, the class of man that the country is asked to do business with, is also a ' matter of prime importance.
I do not know that it is necessary to take up the time of the House further. The issue is an important one. We,certainly did not

refuse the bonus because we felt that shipbuilding should not go on, or because we felt that employment should not be continued, but because we thought that was not the right way of dealing with the matter; and I think that hon. gentlemen as a whole will agree with that conclusion. We did not refuse to include shipbuilding in credits already authorized by the House because we thought that shipbuilding ought not to be carried on but simply because too great an element of risk was involved and because we desired to see that the element of risk should be removed to the greatest possible extent. On the other hand we are anxious, and I know that hon. gentlemen are anxious, that there should be some proper solution to this very vital question, because, of all the manufactured exportable commodities or products that are sent out of this country, there is nothing in which the amount spent for labour is as great as it is in shipbuilding.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.
speechtext:
The
Minister of Finance has told us that twenty-five per cent of the amount will be advanced by the purchaser, twenty-five per cent by the builder and that the Government will become liable for the remaining fifty per cent. My question is: Will these advances be made by the purchaser to the builder before the Government is asked to make any advances?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.
speechtext:
The payments
made by the purchasers are to be made before the Government makes any advance at all. Of course we would have to get ready to do it. The purchaser must pay at least" 10 per cent of the contract entered into; he must then pay at least another 10 per cent at the expiration of six months from the date of the contract, and he has to pay the remaining 5 per cent in nine months after that date. So far as the claim of the builder is concerned that is not a matter, of course, of payment; that is a matter of the builder subordinating his claim to that of the Government. We are leaving the question of what the builder does with the purchaser entirely to one-side. He will have to make his own arrangements; he is not being assisted in that in the slightest degree. The Government always has to come first; and the loan can, never be more than 50 per cent either of the amount of material on hand or of the amount of work done.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.
speechtext:
Will the Government make advances to the builder while the construction is going on, or will
they wait until the builder or the purchaser puts 50 per cent in before they make any advance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.
speechtext: The advances must be made while the construction is going on. The amounts that II mentioned would not, of course, nearly cover the construction of the boat. The construction of the boat will not be completed until the whole 100 per cent is put into that boat. But we start out with the proposition that the Government is never to be committed for more than 50 per cent of the whole, and that it cannot be -committed to five cents until first the 25 per -cent is satisfactorily arranged. It cannot be allowed to stand longer than during -the dates I have given, and not one cent can be advanced until the builder subordinates his -claim for^ that 25 per cent to the Government's claim in respect of any contingent liability that it may ever be responsible for.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.
speechtext:
In other words, the
Government takes a second mortgage. Now what would happen if, after the purchaser had put up 25 ,per -cent in cash and -through the Government's endorsement of the purchaser's note another 50 per cent had been spent, the builder failed, leaving the boat three-quarters completed?
Sir HENRY -DRAYTON: That is one of the reasons why we would not like to say we would do this- with everybody or anybody. We have got to know whom we are dealing with.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.
speechtext:
If you were to make
an error in- judgment what might happen?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.
speechtext: If we were to make an error in judgment we would have on our hands a boat for which 25 per cent in cash had been paid, and we would have to look after the balance.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.
speechtext:
Are these advances to be made subject to any control?
-Sir HENRY DRAYTON: To the fullest control. The matter can only go along in the ordinary manner of shipbuilding. We have to have a naval architect, and advances can only be made and notes can only be endorsed on the -certificate of the architect -the ordinary system of progress certificates arranged either through Lloyds-

maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.
speechtext:
Or the Bureau Veritas?
-Sir HENRY DRAYTON:-or the Bureau Veritas, acting in conjunction with our own department-the purchaser will require

either Lloyd or the Bureau Veritas. We, in addition to that, would require a check hy our own department.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.
speechtext: Is there any interest on deferred payments in this transaction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.
speechtext: The Government's position is that, it advances nothing; it endorses. If there is a default it is the duty of the Government to enforce it against the security, but there is no Government advance at all.

maintopic: GOVERNMENT CREDITS. IN AID OF SHIPBUILDING.
speechtext:
I listened with great
pleasure this afternoon to the Prime Minister who said that it seemed to him there were people in this country and in 'this House who failed to appreciate the financial position in which Canada is at the present time. In bringing in this resolution I am very much afraid that the Minister of Finance will have to be classed among the latter-named people. II am opposed to this legislation absolutely on principle, and also because I think it is ill-advised and dangerous. Now what is the principle that is supposed' to rule the members of this House? That there should be special privileges for none, and equal rights for all. If I go-representing as I do a rural constituency- to the Minister of Finance, and I say, "There is a worthy farmer in my county who wants to put up a new steel barn made by a manufacturer of Montreal, and this manufacturer is quite willing that if he (the farmer) will pay him 25 per cent and will give him a promissory note for another 50 per cent endorsed by my learned and hon. friend the Minister of Finance he (the manufacturer) will take a second mortgage on the property,"-if I go with that proposal to the Minister of Finance will he listen to me for a minute? No. He will say, "That is an impossibility." I think this country has in the past made great mistakes by bonusing industries, either directly by bonuses or indirectly by a system of protection. I believe that that has had the effect of stimulating into precocious economic life many industries of the country before the country was ready for them, to the great loss of Canada and to the very slight benefit, if any, of the industries affected. Now, that is the first principle I want to lay down. Next, we are asked to commit ourselves- after the Minister of Finance has had to tax children's baseballs and skates in order to raise money-to an indirect liability without limit. There is not the slightest limit in this proposal. There is an indirect liabil-
ity. What does the minister say? "The element of risk is removed, we are only going to advance 50 per cent of the value of the ship." Well, before the war, ships could be built for about $50 per ton. I suppose the contracts which will be affected by this legislation will be contracts which will run from $175 to $200 per ton. Let us take $180 as a fair average. Well, ships will not always be built for $180 a ton. The shipping situation, as all other situations iln the world, will regulate itself; and in course of time, even if we make due allowance for the expansion of currency, we will find in a few years that ships can be built for $90 or $100 a ton. What does that mean? It means that our equity in the ships is wilped out altogether. The last Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) made a reputation for himself as the greatest borrowing minister that Canada has known; and if thife legislation goes through, the present Minister of Finance will make a reputation for himself as the greatest loaning Minister of Finance that we have known. I congratulate the 'minister when he tells us that of those credits to Rumania, to Greece, and to Italy, which were approved of by the House in sessions gone by, not all have been spent. I congratulate him upon that. If it has been in his power to prevent the Canadian people from using these credits to a very large extent he deserves thanks from us and I tender thanks to him; but I hope that the amount saved in this direction is not going to be risked in that. Of course the minister will tell us that there is no risk. 'There has never been a man yet who went to a friend to back his promissory note who has not said to him, "Dear Jones, you will never be called upon to meet this note. This note will be met by me at the bank long before it falls due." Now, what does this legislation imply?

speechtext: Qui endosse paie.

speechtext:
The hon. member
for Brome (Mr. McMaster) understands full well that while the Government own the ships they do not operate them. The ships are being operated by private management just the .same as are the Canadian Pacific1 Railway ships.

Who owns the private
management?
Mr. M(MASTER.: Let us try and not camouflage the situation. Those who run our ships are creatures of the Government. If these people took the bit in their teeth and did things which he considered unwise, the Minister of Marine and Fisheries would quickly bring them to book, because he is too much of a business man and has too keen a sense of his responsibility to. allow those men to remain in charge a single day longer if he considered they were doing wrong. I do not want to flatly contradict the minister in .any rude or discourteous manner, but I say the people see through that camouflage. The minister, is, in the ultimate analysis, responsible for the operation of these ships,' and when he gets up in this House and swells with justifiable pride that he ha6 made a profit of 51 per cent in operating those ships after everything has been taken care of, his pride is because of the fact that the gratifying result reflects upon his good management, as he contends, of those ships.
But the point I want to make is this. It is bad enough to own and operate ships even though you may .as compensation for running the risk get what profits there are; but to become mortgage creditors of ships without getting one cent of compensation for the risk you run,-that is Government ownership of ships even worse than what we have at present. I trust that the minister will not proceed with such a piece of vicious legislation. It is unfair ion the face of it. Why should a man who wants to buy a 3,000-ton ship be able to get this concession from the Government while the man who wants to buy a 1,000-ton ship is not able to get it? Why shoiuld a fishermen who wants to get a small schooner of 50, 100 or 200 tons

Or a returned soldier fisherman.	*
Mr. McMASTEiR: Yes, a returned soldier fisherman, as suggested to me by the hon. member for Quebec South (iMr. Power), who is always interested in the welfare of the returned soldier-why should he not be able to get such assistance while other people who want larger boats get' this accommodation? I believe that the policy for Canada to adopt is to have every tub stand on its own bottom, and to have every ship float likewise. I am opposed to this legislation, and I trust that it will not be accepted by the House.	'

I wish also to voice my opposition to this vicious legislation. We are undertaking to do something that no person in Canada outside af a pawn-broker is authorized to do. A banker would not be allowed to take the security that the minister is willing to accept; it would be against the law of the country. A trust company would not be permitted to take the security. No person outside of a pawnbroker could take this security, and we are asked by this Government to reduce the Parliament of Canada to the position of going around backing peoples' notes. It is the most vicious legislation that has ever been presented to this House. It comes right next to the Roumanian loans which were granted a year or two ago, and on which we have not yet received one cent of interest nor one cent of principal. This proposal of the Government to go broadcast throughout the world and back the notes of Tom, Dick and Harry is so absurd that I am surprised that any minister would allow himself to, be inveigled into it by any set of interests. What have we to gain by it? We are told [DOT]that it will mean employment for some [DOT]men. Well, what are we going to do when other interests rap at the door and ask for a guarantee to employ their men? What are we going to do if the farmer asks for this kind of assistance? If he wants to buy a horse, why should you not endorse his note as well as the note of some man who wants to buy a ship? What is to be gained for Canada? Absolutely nothing. Our credit is surely not so good that we can afford to go round endorsing notes at this time. We cannot gain anything; we shall merely increase the cost of living. We tell the returned soldier that we are not in a position to re-establish him by making him a loan on his fishing boat or

fishing nets, but we go to foreign countries and make loans to their citizens in order to enable them to come here and buy ships. Mr. Chairman, this thing is so absurd that when I read the resolution on the Order Paper I wondered whether I was in Parliament or not, but when I remembered some of the Government's past actions I was not surprised. I would not be surprised at anything they might do; they are irresponsible; they represent no one but themselves.
