If I were permitted to take every member of the Government, down to the elm tree at the gate and hang them to the limbs of that tree, I do not believe it would be possible for you to get a jury of twelve men in this country who would not vote me a bonus.

I object very strongly to the bringing forward of this resolution at so late a day in the session. I regard it as a breach of faith, in a certain sense, because we were assured a few days ago that all the important legislation had been, brought, down. This is one of the most important measures that has been brought down during the present session. The amount of liability involved is unlimited. We do not say in the resolution that we will build one ship, ten ships or one hundred ships; there is no end to the assistance that the Minister of Marine and the Minister of Finance may give under this resolution. One of the things we will have to do before we go further with this resolution is to place a limit on these gentlemen. They have already invested 870,000,000 of the country's money in ships; whether it is- a good investment remains to be seen. The minister tells us that it is a good investment, hut it will take time to prove that it is. It is noticeable that private enterprise is not coming forward to build ships at the same rate that the minister has been paying for the ships built by the Government. Why is it that private enterprise does not take hold of this matter? Is there no money in Canada? Have the people of this country no money to invest in ships? Is there any man in Canada who will put his money in ships at the rate of $200 a ton for tramp vessels? Will the minister himself do it? Has the Minister of Marine (Mr. Ballantyne) invested one dollar of his own money in a scheme of this kind at these prices? We all know that the prices are extravagant; it is clear to everybody that they cannot last. Shipping is increasing at an enormous rate. The tonnage of the

world is now about as large as it was before the war; it is increasing day by day and it will not be long until it becomes as cheap as it was before the war. A great change will take place within a year or two; a mortgage for a given amount on a ship that is built at $200 a ton to-day may not be worth half as much two or three years hence. No industry is so hazardous as the shipping industry; it will be very difficult for the minister to protect himself against what may happen in this regard.
Now, the principal argument that the Minister of Finance has put forward is with regard to labour. He informs us that a large number of men are employed in the shipyards of this country, and he assumes that if the Government does not come to the rescue of these shipyards and keep them going at these extravagant prices these men will be out of employment. I do not think his argument is sound. My hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) stated the facts correctly when he pointed out that labour was scarce and employment plentiful; that men are wanted in all walks of business. If
25,000	men are now engaged in the shipbuilding industry the other industries are open to them; that is not a good reason why the Government should embark on this extravagant proposal. The minister Will have to present some stronger argument in order to make out a case for the adoption of this resolution. It appears that he intends to deal with foreign buyers, people about whom we know nothing. We know who the shipyard people are, but we do not know who the buyers from outside are. We cannot very well know who they are; they may be men of straw or they may be speculators. We are giving them our money; we are endorsing their notes. It would be much more to the point if we assisted our own people at home. Why has the Government no shipbuilding policy? When the leader of the Government (Sir Robert Borden) ran his election in 1911 he promised the people of Canada a shipbuilding policy, but no such policy has been forthcoming. We have a shipowning policy just now; we own ships at very extravagant prices; but we have no shipbuilding policy, no policy under which the people of this country can themselves embark upon shipbuilding. Surely the building of ships by the Government cannot be characterized as a shipbuilding policy. A national policy is a policy under which the people of Canada are enabled to embark in the business of Canada. But this Government seem to have no ability to frame a 253.J
policy by which the people can embark in the shipbuilding industry. We would all be very glad to see them do it. We want Canada to be a ship-owning country, but those of us who have any idea of business feel that public ownership is not the kind of ownership that will succeed in the shipbuilding industry. I think we have made a mistake in going so far as we have in regard to the matter. I feel pretty sure that if we accept this proposal we will later on have a lot of financial shipwrecks on our hands. I am opposed to this measure and will vote against it.

I wish to place myself on record as absolutely opposed to the proposal made by this resolution. It is only a few hours since we asked Parliament to lend a few hundred thousand dollars to returned soldiers in order that we might get increased production, which is so much needed in this country and throughout the world to-day. We wanted to enable returned men to produce food from the sea as well as from the land-because both these lines of production are equally necessary. I pointed out this afternoon that the production of food from the sea was quite as important as the production of food from the land. This proposal is merely giving protection to a certain class of people or to certain companies who will promise to do the best they can for the returned soldier by giving him employment. At this moment, in the present condition of the world, as it has been so well described by my hon. friend (Mr. McMaster) and other hon. members who have followed him, we know that the cost of shipbuilding is at the highest possible pitch and that in a few years those ships will not be worth fifty per cent of the money that we are undertaking the responsibility of advancing to-day. We want to keep our young men, more particularly, from the cities and keep them on the farms as much as possible. Whenever in this Parliament we ask for advances to assist the producers of the food which is so - much needed throughout the world today, we are told that we had better wait and see what conditions will be like in a few years from -now. The proposition to make advances to soldiers engaged in the fishing industry was, at the advice of the Prime Minister, withdrawn, to the great regret, I am sure, of the mover of that amendment, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Peck), the Prime Minister's reason being that, after all, no good results would be achieved this session and that possibly at the next session something might be done

for the returned soldier. I am taking the liberty to-night of 'asking Parliament to accept the advice given by the Prime Minister this afternoon and to allow this -matter to remain until the opening of next session which, we hope, will be not longer than six months from now if the Government is still in power. If the Government is rejected by the people of Canada, by that time the new Parliament will have a new mandate and will act in accordance with the requirements of the people. I am opposed to this bonus in disguise to a few companies which, if they be in earnest should be able to get, from the banks of Canada, the advances necessary for their enterprise. The banks offer credit to almost any enterprise that the industrial people of this country wish to undertake in order to send the products of their industry *to other parts of the world. The banks will do the same thing for the construction of ships, and there is nothing the banks of Canada would be more apt to encourage than the construction of ships on the basis of financial conditions. Therefore, with all the regard which I have for the Minister of Finance (Sir -Henry Drayton), in whose hand's this -resolution has been placed

 placed in his hands, I presume, because he is known to have more of the kind regard of members of the Opposition than, perhaps, other hon. members opposite,-I cannot possibly -accede to his request at the present moment, and I hope a delay will be granted. A delay of six months more will not seriously affect shipping construction in the world to-day. We know that we have enough ships for the next six months to *meet the imperative demands of the commercial world. Therefore, we should wait until next session, until the people of Canada may have time to cogitate over this offer and study the question of their appreciation or disapproval of such -a project. Then, when we come next session with this project, we shall come enlightened by the declaration of public opinion.
Mr. BALL-AjNTYNE :	It is just possible
that hon. members have not quite grasped the statement made by my colleague the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton). Members of the committee are aware that the Government shipbuilding programme is at an end. We have a proposal submitted to the Government that France, which is badly in need of tonnage, wishes to have millions of dollars worth of ships constructed in our yards. As regards the 50 per cent that the Government are asked to advance, I want to point out, as the Minister

of Finance did, that first of all the buyer gives his note, and the Minister of Finance will see to it that that buyer is financially good. After that note has been taken from the buyer, it is handed to the shipbuilder for his endorsation. We have first of all the buyer's note, secondly, we have the endorsation on the buyer's note of the shipbuilder, and thirdly, the Government have a mortgage for the full amount of the ships that are going to be ordered in Canada. I really do not see that the Government or this Parliament or the country runs any risk whatever in advancing fifty per cent of the money, taking good security in addition to the mortgage on the ships, which mortgage is a first mortgage for the total amount of the note. -The Minister of Finance and your humble servant will see to it that the buyer is financially good; that the shipbuilder to whom the contracts are going to be given, is financially good. With a good note from a financially sound buyer, that note being endorsed by financially strong Canadian shipbuilders, and with a mortgage on the full value of the ship, I should like hon. members to,tell me what risk the Government of Canada runs in advancing fifty per cent of the construction cost. If we wait until six months from now, as my hon. friend (Mr. Turgeon) has suggested, that would be too late. The shipbuilding industry of Canada has no protection whatever. 'Canadians have demonstrated that they can build ships equally as good as are built in the United ' Kingdom can and at as low a cost. I will admit, when the tonnage of the world becomes more evened up than it is now, the cost of shipbuilding is bound to go down; but I for one do not for one moment admit that we shall ever see steel ships built again for 850 a ton. I doufot very much if we shall ever see them built for $90 a ton as the hon. member for Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) has suggested. But even so: the average contract price of these ships would probably run from $170 to $175 a ton; and supposing ships went down to half that value,' .the Government has :a mortgage-on the full amount of the ships. If I were going back into business and did happen to be a member of the Government, as I am at this moment, and that was put up to me as a business proposition, not only would I accept it, but I would recommend it to my board of directors. It is a sound, clean-cut business proposition to bring into this country millions of dollars, to keep our seventeen yards in Canada busy for two or three years, and to keep employed
i

50,000	skilled Canadian workmen, a very large percentage of whom are returned soldiers. I have no hesitation whatever in endorsing fully the views of my colleague, the Minister of Finance and also the resolution that is now before the committee.
Mr. MeMAST.ER:	To what extent is it
contemplated that endorsement should be made?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is a very difficult matter to state. My opinion is that the Government would not be called upon to advance on a fifty-fifty basis any more than $25,000,000 or $30,000,000 at the outside, covering a period of, say, three years.

Has
the minister considered where he is going to get the money from?

This resolution, I take
it, disposes of the suggestion we have seen in the newspapers from time to time that the Government might embark on some policy of subsidizing shipbuilding in this country. That policy would be, in my judgment, absolutely bad, and the policy proposed by the Minister of Finance in this resolution does not fall very far short of the other so far as its badness and unsoundness is concerned. I am opposed to the proposal embodied in this resolution. It is true that we are not handing over to shipbuilding concerns sums of money in actual cash by way of subsidy. What we are doing is pledging the credit of Canada to assist in the building of these ships. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine argues that there is no risk in it. He states that he and the Minister of Finance, who would have to do with the matter, will see to it that only purchasers and builders who are sound financially will come in under this scheme. I ask my hon. friend, if the purchaser is sound financially, and if the builder is sound financially why is it necessary to ask the Government to give this assistance? If they cannot finance the construction themselves, if they have not the ready capital to put into it, why cannot they take their notes to the banks and raise the necessary money? The very fact that the Government are asked to endorse these notes constitutes an element of doubt. It is an old story we have heard to-night as to there being no risk in the transaction. We have had railroads built in this country, and the arguments were advanced at that time that there was no risk in the Government guaranteeing the bonds of these railways,
that the railways were sure to pay and that they would furnish employment to labour. The same arguments that were advanced in favour of guaranteeing the bonds of the railways have been advanced in support of this proposal to-night. Every one knows the result of our guaranteeing the bonds of these railways. The enterprises have fallen down and the country has had to step in and make good its guarantees on the bonds. With the burden of debt that rests on this country, with our financial commitments away beyond what any one would have dreamt of six years ago, is it wise at the present time for us to contemplate any increase in the indirect liabilities of this country? I do not think' it is.
Again, there is a substantial argument against this proposal on the ground that it is a discrimination. Why should shipbuilders and ship purchasers from foreign countries be entitled to this assistance? Are the Government adopting this as a permanent policy? If they are prepared to give assistance to the purchasers of ships by endorsing their notes so that they can get the money they require, are they prepared to give this assistance also to other industrial enterprises that want to set up in business and give employment to labour? I would like the Minister of Finance to answer that question. I say that we cannot afford to -exercise discrimination of this kind If I want to build a pulp mill and have only a certain amount of money and I come to the Government and ask them to endorse my notes in order that I may secure the necessary funds to build the mill, will the Government assist me as they propose to assist these purchasers of ships? Will they give the same assistance to other industries? I say that the country has no right to embark on a policy of that kind particularly in the present state of our Finances.

Did not the Farmers'
Co-operative Elevator Company in the province of Alberta get all their credit from the Government of that province?

My hon. friend is not
very familiar with the history of that enterprise.

I am perfectly familiar with if.
Mr. -CRERAR:	I still submit that my
hon. friend does not know what he is talk-

ing about when he makes that statement, and I will tell him why. When these elevators were built there was more than sufficient capital stock subscribed to pay their whole cost, and 20 per cent
12 m. of it had to be paid up. The Government held1 not only a mortgage on the elevators for the advances it gave, but also the subscribed stock. They were 200 per cent secured on the enterprise. My hon. friend surely cannot be serious when he makes the statement that this is a similar enterprise. I say again that this proposal is a discrimination, and I want to know, and I think the House and the country are entitled to know, whether this is the settled policy of the Government. Is the Government willing to give this assistance to other enterprises? I think that is a fair and a reasonable question to ask the Minister of Finance. We cannot have too much regard for the financial condition of this country at the present time. I say that our policy should be retrenchment, and again retrenchment, in this country. We should bring our expenditure within our income, nationally, and we must make headway in reducing the national debt. I say that faced with that debt, it is not a sound policy to add to the indirect liability of this country by the $25,000,000 or $30,000,000 which the Minister of Marine 'and Fisheries says will probably be involved in this proposal. I submit that it is not a sound policy for this country to embark upon.

I happened to be in the legislature of Alberta at the time the Act authorizing the loan to the Farmers' Co-Operative Elevator Company in that province was passed. The Farmers' Co-Operative Elevator Company came to the Government, got their credit, and got their money, and the credit of the province of Alberta is being used for that particular industry in that particular province at this particular time. If you go into he province of Saskatchewan yau will find that the credit of that province was also used in connection with the elevators there. If my hon. friend will look over the history of the western provinces during the last few years, he will find that this Federal Government was the one Government in the Dominion of Canada which advanced loans for the purchase of seed grain by the farmers of the West. So far as the transportation of the products of Western Canada are concerned, I think it is the duty of this Government to establish a mercantile marine under our own control, so that we shall not be dependent upon the shipping of any other part of the

Empire, or of any foreign country. I think if this Government is to be congratulated upon anything, it is that they are willing to render assistance for the purpose for which this resolution is introduced.

The situation is wholly
different between this proposal and the proposals for giving assistance in the building of elevators in the provinces of Alberta and 'Saskatchewan. Bet me repeat, in those provinces the Government had not only the elevators as security, but they had the subscribed stock that was unpaid, for more than the whole cost of the enterprise. My hon. friend's argument falls down in another particular. He asks, is not this a good policy to assist in building up a mercantile marine which will be able to carry our western grain? But who will the ships be built for? The Minister of Marine and Fisheries says they will be built for the French Government. What this Government is really doing is assisting foreign countries to build ships which will be used in competition with our own mercantile marine.

Does not my hon. friend admit that the Farmers' Co-Operative Elevator Company in the province of Alberta went to the Government of that province and got legislation passed enabling them to get money on the strength of the credit of the province of Alberta? He contradicted me a minute ago and said it was not so.

I did not.
Mr. TWIEEDIEi I was in the legislature when the legislation wlas passed.
The Government did give them assistance.

That was simply my point.
Glome hon. MEMBERS: Carried.
I want to emphasize that point,

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I am sorry that I must call the hon. member (IMr. Tweedie) to order. We are not discussing what took place in Alberta in connection with elevators.

I shall not depart from your ruling, Mr. Chairman, in the slighest. What we are discussing is the advisability of this Government rendering assistance to any industry, and as a reason for considering whether we should grant that assistance or not it was submitted that no other similar class of industry had received sup-

port from any government. I pointed out that the very industry with which the hon. member for Marquette was connected and the company oif which he was manager endeavoured to get control of all these elevators and received government support both in the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta.

Coming as I do from the Maritime Provinces, I would be expected to be one who would be warmly , interested in all forms of maritime enterprise. I represent a shipbuilding constituency. 1 am in a larger degree than perhaps some hon. gentlemen around me in sympathy with the efforts that the Minister of Marine has made in regard to giving us a fleet of Canadian ships. I would like it if I could support the present proposition. But'I am bound to say that I think it has not been well prepared, that it is a hastily devised piece of legislation and that the Government would be wise if they would take a few months more to consider it. It is a hastily devised piece of legislation because it is not many days since the Prime Minister informed us that we would have no more important legislation presented to the House. That is the best evidence that it has been prepared hurriedly tta meet some alleged emergency. It was under circumstances of this kind that the Government, in the last stages of last session, brought forward the Board of Commerce Bill and passed it. Nobody understood it or what would be the result of it; nobody knows what good it has accomplished up to this time or what good it is likely to be in the future. This legislation is prepared in a hurry-scurry way. I would frankly say that that I have not had an opportunity of considering it at any great length and I do not believe other members of the House have had opportunity. We have had a bare quorum ion the Government side of the House for most of the evening, many members are absent and a great many others have probably gone home. At all events we have a very slim House to take up at this late hour such a very large and important measure.
There are a number of the details of the measure that strike me as being rather odd but possibly they may be amended. In so far as the object of the Bill is to encourage ship building, and to give employment to people, it commends itself to me, but I see some difficulties in the way. The aid that is to be granted is to be in the form of a guarantee. I do not like guarantees. We
have given guarantees to some railway companies. I hiave always objected to guarantees, although in the case of different railway enterprises they seemed -to be inevitable and I must take my share of responsibility for some of those guarantees. But if this is something that the Government must assist, I for one would rather lend the money outright than see the Government get mixed up with notes. To have the notes of shipbuilders guaranteed by the Dominion Government floating around in this way seems to be a rather undignified proceeding and I would rather lend them the money outright.
I notice that a ship, to be able to take advantage of this legislation must be of
3,000	tons. I represent' a shipbuilding community where they build vessels very much less than 3,000 tons, and I have no doubt many excellent workmen might say: "If the Government is assisting somebody in France to build a ship of 3,000 tons why can it not assist somebody in France to build a ship of 1,000 tons or 2,000 tons 6uch as we can build in Nova Scotia?" This Bill seems clearly to imply that its application will be limited to steel shipbuilding although it is not so expressed. I would like to ask the Minister of Finance if it contemplates the recognition of wooden shipbuilding as well.
Sir HENRY D'RAYTON: No, steel only.

That is going to confine the operations of the Bill to a limited number of shipyards in the country. I do not undervalue these shipyards; I am glad we have them, and I wish them all success and prosperity. But there are hundreds of shipyards scattered over Nova Scotia and New Brunswick that will not get any benefit whatever from this Bill, and those concerned with these enterprises are very likely to ask the same question as that which has been asked by the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar). If this Bill passes in its present shape the Government can carry it on forever and guarantee as much money as it pleases. There is no limit as to the time and there is no limit to the amount which is to be guaranteed. These are both certainly very serious objections. Then I notice that while it is provided that ships are to be insured, nothing is said as to who is to do the insuring, whether the Government or the owners. I take it for granted that when my hon. friend's attention has been drawn to this fact he will see that it is made clear; but there is nothing said as

to who is to do the insuring. Another point is that the notes are to run for four or five years. Is there any provision for renewing them? Still another point is that although we are to get our money back we are not to get any interest. As I read the Bill all we can claim is that we get back the amount that we have given in the shape of our endorsement. We have given our endorsement, we have given our credit, but we are not going to get back any interest if any of these notes should be in default-because I do not see any provision for the payment of interest. If the notes are taken up the purchaser pays the interest and we are protected; but if the notes should fall into the hands of the Government by default I see no provision by which the Government can get back interest. All they get back is the principal sum. There are many of these small details that one might bring to the attention of the Government. But in addition to that the general ground might be taken that at this very late stage in the session it would be utterly impossible for the Government to give the time that should be given to such an important measure as this. It is still more impossible for this Parliament to give it the consideration that ,its importance demands. I trust that the Government will try to find some other means of aiding the shipbuilding industry even if they have to take another session to do it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Ihave.no quarrel with some of the remarks of hon. gentlemen across the way.. The only thing I complain about is that they have not grasped what we are trying to do. Take the position of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Crerar). H says this is discrimination; that the same thing would not be done for another industry. Well, it is discrimination. We have put up in credits over $400,000,000 for the removal and sale of farm products to the extent of one hundred per cent. Of course that is discrimination. It was done and there was no mistake-I do not think the hon. member for Marquette will say it was a mistake; he will say that it was a good thing that Canada kept functioning, it was a good thing that we kept going, it was a good thing that there was a market retained for our farmers.
' If it was a bad thing to have a market for our farmers, if it was a bad thing to allow the farmers to produce and be able to sell their products then it was a mistake, but the hon. member for Marquette will not say so. It is discrimination forsooth, because we -are doing something which I

do not think we have ever tried to do be-r fore. That is to see that no one gets anything out of this until we -get our money. With respect to the blanket mortgage that the hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has referred to in connection with a railroad, of course there is a great deal of distinction there. They get their mortgage, they get their money, they have the whole thing open, and we assume the responsibility and the liability. Take the case the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) speaks of when he say3 that the cost Of boat building is coming down. I think he is right to this extent- I think the cost of boat building will be coming down. But the hon. member says the prices to-day are high. He puts the -price at $180 a ton. I am not quarrelling with that at all. But he say-s that price will ibe cut in two, and if it is cut in two "your whole equity is gone." But we are not dealing in the equity, we are dealing in the mortgage.
Mr. MoMASTER: But you have no margin left.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Talking about equity, it is the other man that is cut out and the -country iB left there with its security which my learned friend himself says is equal to the whole amount of our debt. So far as interest is concerned, as I say, we are only endorsers. The hon. member for Shelburne and Queen's asks, "What is going to happen, if we have to make good?" Well, the only thing that will happen if we have to make good is that we foreclose -that ib all-and we are entitled to our interest -on the overdue debt just as much as any overdue debt is entitled to interest on it. In other words, from the very moment (that we have to put up any money our interest accrues.

I heard some mention of a splendid order coming from France. Has there been any idea of getting the French Government to endorse any of these notes to secure the Canadian Government in the guarantees it is going to give?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The proposition at one time was that the French Government would put up Fxenoh Government bonds. A .further proposition has been that some of the best banks in France would put up their obligations. The whole difficulty has been merely one o-f exchange.
There is one thing I should mention: When we come to the discussion of the Bill

to be founded on this resolution, if it is approved, I am going to propose limitations both as to the amount of the risk to be taken and also as to the time of the operation of the Bill. It is not intended that this legislation should allow any new industry to be built up, it is not intended to start any new yards; it is merely intended to see, if we possibly can, that a very large number of very estimable Canadian workmen are not thrown out of employment. It just so happens that there are still skilled men, it just so happens that they are accustomed to this kind of work, it just so happens that during the present period of shipbuilding they have learned this trade, and we want to so provide that they will continue Ito receive employment.

Probably nothing can be added from this side of the House to what has already (been said, but I think it is right to oppose this measure. I think the measure is bad business, I think it is absolutely unsound, I do not think that there is any principle of business upon which it can be justified. Therefore such legislation should never have been brought into this House, much less brought in at this late hour of the session. We were very willing to take a hand, and hurry along and. get through with the original business of the House that had been before us for weeks and months. Now, at this very stage, when we have already practically wound up the business of the session, this new proposal is brought in. It is absolutely new-I have never heard of anything like it in Canada before; that the Government of this country should begin to endorse notes for somebody. If I went home to-morrow, took the hustings, and began telling the people that this Government at Ottawa are undertaking to endorse the notes of somebody they do not know-if they do know they will not tell us-and are going to put up thirty millions of money (according to the Minister of Marine the obligation may go to thirty millions) endorsing the notes of this man, nobody would believe me. The people would say, "You are insane. (Nobody on earth would do a thing like that." Here we are face to face with the Government to-night, with the Minister of Finance at its head, and he will not tell us whose note he has in his pocket. It is in blank I suppose; I do not know whether there is even a two-cent stamp on it; but I assure my hon. friend that though he endorses it himself I would hesitate to give him the stamp to put on it. In all
seriousness, Mr. Chairman, I want to know to whom the people of this country are going to turn for protection. Surely the Canadian people who send us here have a right to know the facts. I appeal to men sitting in this House-men that are sane, are serious, and understand business principles. We are told that there is no money to spare, that we are in debt, we are shcrt and cannot meet our bills. When any person comes to Parliament looking for money for the returned soldiers in any shape whatsoever, the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White), is called to stand up to rebutt their claim. The Government would not be satisfied with any less important witness. They called that hon. gentleman to the stand, and, under the solemnity of an oath, he told the special committee that were dealing with the matter, and told the people of this country, that it was absolutely out of the question to think oc spending any money on the returned soldiers because we did not have it. Not only was Sir Thomas White called to the stand, but so were the Deputy Minister of Finance and every other man whose word was worth having. And the conclusion the committee drew from that evidence was that no matter how kindly we felt towards the returned soldier, no matter how much we would like to help him and his family, and put him on the highway to success, we did not have the money with which to do it. And, as has been said to-day-I think by the Prime Minister himself-we must cut our coat according to our cloth. Now we have come to a position when the coat and the cloth are any size whatever and there are no limitations of any kind. I want to ask the Minister of Marine-who is a business man and who seems to have a hobby in the shipbuilding business: If shipbuilding will not stand upon its own bottom to-day when is it going to do so? The prices for shipbuilding are at the top notch. Shipbuilding is in ia better condition to-day than it will be five years, or seven years from now. The minister says the people concerned are of good financial standing they are men of high credit, they, are men with respect to whom simply as a matter of form-for the purposes of identification I suppose-the minister has placed his name on the back of the note. That is all. Well, if they are such good business men, if they need this assistance in a prosperous time for shipbuilding like the present, what is going to happen when the prices of ships come tumbling about their ears? What becomes of our mortgage and of our security? We

should make up our minds to stay here all night, all day to-morrow, and every day this week, to stand at the door of the treasury of this country, and defend it against the most outrageous onslaught that was ever made upon it.
It stands without parallel. We have had to go into debt to the tune of $75,000,000 to embark in the shipbuilding business, and now we have become so hilarious that we are willing to endorse our competitor's securities. We say to him, "Why, this is easy. We are doing splendidly. We made $5,000,000 last year. Certainly we did not allow anything for depreciation, but we had new ships and we made 5J per cent. Come along, Sir. You have no money, but we will endorse your paper." That is the temporary intoxication in which the Minister of Marine and Fisheries finds himself, and he drags along with him the new Minister of Finance, who really has very little knowledge of what is going on. We are asked to walk home at this hour of the night and let those honest gentlemen get their hands deep into the Treasury. We stand here possibly "like a voice crying in the wilderness," for we are not in a majority; but it is our duty to raise our feeble voice against this unbusinesslike proposition.
The facts of the case 'have been presented to hon. members and to the Government. What more can we do? But we do say, hon. gentlemen, that we will remember these things, that we will tell the people about them, and that if the Government turn us down because they have a majority and take this money contrary to every principle of good business', we will "appeal to Caesar." We will tell the returned soldier and his widow, and bis children, "This refusal of money to you was a mere camouflage. The very night that they turned down your proposition they voted $30,000,000 to some unknown Dago from across the Atlantic to build ships." Anybody can build ships if we furnish the money. Anybody apparently can get the Minister of Finance to endorse a blank note, with a bad stamp on the corner of it, and then build ships and sell them, and if he has anything left over so much the better; If he has not he has lost nothing. I shall have no hesitation in telling this to the people because we have no evidence to the contrary.
I ask those members older than the ministers who are facing us to-night if ever they heard of a $30,000,000 proposition being submitted to any Parliament, much less to

this Parliament, on such bareboned, meagre information as has been furnished to us to-night? I appeal to hon. gentlemen opposite for their own sakes to have some respect for this House and to let us have a breathing spell at least to find out something about this thing before they attempt to force' down our throats such an unbusinesslike proposition.

Mr. Chairman, it was not my intention to take part in this discussion, but this question has worked upon me to such an extent that I feel it my duty to declare myself as unalterably opposed to it. The hon. Minister of Finance, likewise the h'on. Minister of Marine and Fisheries told the House that they did not think we grasped the idea; but if any one is deceived I think it is the hon. gentlemen themselves. It is not my policy to endeavour to wilfully stall any legislation, but I would ask: What public sentiment has been presented to this Government to launch this proposal? Or are they, in a spirit of autocracy, taking it upon themselves to present this proposal as a policy good for the Dominion? I am sure that if the people were allowed to stand here to-night and declare their opinion upon this policy, they would condemn it wholeheartedly, and they would condemn also the members who advocate it. I am sure that at this time the people are not willing that their credit should be pledged any further until their own financial conditions have been brought nearer to the point where they can understand and 'handle them.
We have been asked to advance money before, but this proposal is far and away removed from any similar proposal that has been heretofore discussed in this House. I listened to the plea of the Minister of Finance when he was presenting his Budget to this House and showing why he ought to have more revenue through the medium of luxury taxes and other taxes. But I did not think when we were trying to discover ways and means of raising that revenue that the credit of this country was to be used in the manner suggested here to-night.
The argument has been advanced that this proposal will provide labour for some thousands of men. A few weeks ago a modest request was made by me to have a few miles of railway built in my constituency, and I was told that the labour for that work could not be secured. Now we see how the argument is being used when it suits the purpose of this Government, for to-night they say that all kinds of labour is available

for certain things. I like consistency, but I fail to see any in such an argument. I wish to particularly endorse, the sentiments expressed by the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) and to place myself on record as opposed to this resolution.

The Minister of Finance in his first statement told us that some 23,500 were employed in these shipyards. Is that the total number of men employed in steel and wooden shipyards, or in steel shipyards only?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In steel shipyards only.
We were also advised that a. great many of those men were returned soldiers. I would like to know what proportion.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I can only give to the hon. member the information that has been furnished to me by the shipbuilders. They state that about 25 per cent of the 23,500 men are returned soldiers. I might be allowed to add that great pressure has been brought to bear upon the Government by returned soldiers to do something to keep shipbuilding going.
Would the hon. gentleman be in favour of this proposal if it extended to wooden ships?

I have said that we ought
to have further time to consider this resolution. I am not in a position to give a decided answer whether I am in favour of it or not, but I certainly am opposed to the resolution as it reads now. There is discrimination in this resolution between the different shipbuilding industries, and that is not a good policy for this Government to pursue. They ought to adopt a permanent policy which would treat all shipyards alike. There are 23,500 men engaged in the steel shipbuilding industry, and perhaps another 25,000 men engaged in other industries connected with shipbuilding. Moreover, in the wooden shipbuilding business on the Pacific and Atlantic coasts an additional 5f),000 men are employed in the yards, in cutting timber, in making sails, and in doing other work in connection with the building of ships. It is not fair to pick out one class of shipyards and accord to them different treatment from that accorded to others.
In Nova Scotia we have been building during the past six months vessels for French account-that is, vessels which were ordered or contracted for by French buyers and which have been taken delivery of, or
Carried.

Just for that, this resolution will not carry for two hours. I am willing to stay here all night, and if hon. gentlemen opposite do not wish to listen to this discussion, they can go outside somewhere or try to behave themselves. They cannot get legislation through by calling "carried", and we are not going to be bluffed by any hon. member opposite. The resolution reads:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to provide that in any case where a person (hereinafter called the "purchaser") has entered into a contract with a shipbuilder for the building in Canada of a vessel of not less than three thousand tons.
As my hon. friend (IMr. Fielding) said, this portion of the resolution is certainly not well drafted, and the Government should seriously consider the advisability of amendr ing it so as to cover vessels of any size which any shipbuilder may build. Under all the circumstances, the Minister of Finance, in fairness to the members of this committee and to the country, should not press this resolution to-night. A delay of a day or two will not make any difference, and although I, and other members of the House, have mac|e plans with the idea of getting through the business of this House the latter part of this week or early next week, if the Minister of Finance will leave this *matter over I am willing to stay here all next week in order that hon. members may have an opportunity of studying and properly digesting this resolution. But, under present conditions, II cannot support the resolution, and I do not think it is in the interest of the country that the resolution should go through.

There are two sides to every question. I have, perhaps, had occasion to look into this question more than some of my hon. friends, because it was my privilege to form part of delegations that came to interview the Government about getting subsidies to maintain shipbuilding in Canada. I think it was during last summer that delegates from fourteen yards out of the seventeen came here and gave the Government facts and figures. They showed that from forty to fifty million dollars were invested in shipyards in Canada, and that under present conditions of exchange with various countries and present conditions of traffic in this country, unless a bonus or subsidy was given per ton deadweight, or, l think, per horse-power, the shipyards would have to close. In the riding which it is my privilege to represent, there are two shipyards and they have never lacked work. One of them has always taken contracts from foreign countries. To-day, they have contracts, and they can have contracts for thousands of tons of shipping, but the difficulty is that the purchasers of the ships will have to pay five or six times the price of a ship if they place orders in Canada, on account of the depreciation of the currency. France offered those shipbuilders contracts provided the shipbuilders would give France time so as to give an opportunity to the currency to recuperate. This is the obstacle which stands in the way to-day. The Frenchman does not want to pay five times the price, as at the present rate a ship of 7,200 tons would cost over a million dollars. I may say, en passant, that all the contracts which I have had occasion to see-and I have seen six or seven from the Three Rivers shipyards- were at $170 a ton, payable in American currency. That means for the Frenchman a depreciation of about 22 francs to the dollar instead of five. Those people say: We will give you the contract; but on the other hand, as you are getting the benefit of the labour and we are paying you your money, you should extend us a line of credit of 50 per cent so as to give our currency an opportunity to recover and so as not to ruin us. Otherwise, they would have to pay $4,000,000 for a ship worth $1,000,000. This is being done for the purpose of maintaining in this country an industry which will shortly be in a position to compete with the same industry in any other part of the world. We must not forget that our shipbuilding industry is new; that at the start it cost more in Canada to build a ship, because our workmen were not

skilled and the yards were not as well equipped as they are to-day. There are forty or fifty million dollars that will cease producing in this country, that will be a dead loss to the owners because shipbuilding will have to cease, unless we get further contracts, the Government having completed their shipbuilding programme. My friends may think a better way would be to loan the money. That is a matter of opinion. The main point is this: Are we going to let the shipbuilding business in Canada go to the wall? If the answer is in the negative, I say that we have to provide some means of keeping these shipyards going. If our dollar was ,at par in the different countries of the world, thp shipyards of this country w'ould not require a solitary cent from any one in order to carry on. I have talked this matter over with bankers and they state that in view of the large advances that will be required to enable the shipyards to carry out their orders, and in view of the crop which will soon have to be moved-and which, from all signs, is going to be abundant-they haven't the money to advance. The Minister of Finance has said that this proposal will involve from $20,000,000 to S30.no0.000. Bankers in our oart. of the country with whom I have discussed this matter say that it would be too great an obligation for the banks to assume at this time.
It would be no better for us to make a loan. In the present case we have the note of the purchaser, and the Government reserves to itself the right to ascertain his financial condition. If it is not good the Government will not endorse his note. If his credit is good, the Government say: We want to help you along, we will give The adverse exchange a chance to rectify itself, and in the meantime we will enable you to carry on. These people will be able to repay the loan, but they would not be able to pay five times that amount, which is what they would have to pay if they went ahead by themselves at the present rates of exchange. I am sorry to part with my friends, but I am going to support this ' resolution, because from the bottom of my heart I am satisfied that it is absolutely necessary to enable our yards to carry on.
I think it is in the public interest that these men who have become efficient in this kind of work should maintain the shipbuilding industry in Canada. It might be said that I am favouring this resolution because there are shipyards in my riding. Yes, there are, and they have enabled me to ascertain

the conditions in the industry and form an opinion, and I have expressed my honest opinion as I view the matter. I regret that we cannot all see eye to eye on this matter, but I am going to support the resolution as I believe it is in the public interest. If there is anything deficient in the wording of the resolution, we can suggest improvements. If my friends think it would be well to set a limit on the time or the amount, we can discuss that when the Bill comes down. From my own knowledge 1 know that the need is pressing and that .aid should be given at once. Otherwise, a calamity might hit our country through the shipyards being unable to carry on.

There is no man in this House. I would hate to oppose more than my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau), but I am absolutely opposed to the principle of this resolution. The principle is wrong. The Government have made no attempt to explain where they got the idea of this principle of guaranteeing the notes of people outside the country, or inside the country for that matter. Where is there a precedent for it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are lots of precedents. I will give my hon. friend one that he is fond of, because I know he supports everything from the West. I would refer him to chapter 13 of the statutes of 1913 of the province of Alberta.	.
I am speaking of a nation, not of a province, or a town, or a village.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My hon. friend wanted a' precedent. Section 31 of the Act I have just cited reads:
The Lieutenant Governor in Council is hereby authorized from time to time and on such terms and conditions as may be agreed on with the company to loan to the company for the purpose of aiding- in the acquisition, erection, extension or remodelling of any elevator or elevators a sum not to exceed eighty-five per cent of the estimated cost of the said elevator or elevators or of such extension or remodelling.

That is all right for a
province. No, it is not right for anybody, but it is a different matter entirely in the case of a province or a town. I remember reading that when Sir John Macdonald was in Washington when the negotiations on the treaty of 1871 were being carried on, when the American plenipotentiary wanted him to take a cash payment in lieu of the fishery rights of Canada, he refused. After

discussing it for several days he finally suggested that the difficulty might be overcome if the British Government would guarantee the bonds of a railway in Canada. The plenipotentiary of Great Britain of that day, without hesitation said, "No, Great Britain will not guarantee the bonds of a railway in Canada. I tell you at once, it is impossible." I think Gladstone was in power at that time, and he said the proposal could not be - considered. They (did discuss, however, giving a cash bonus or a loan, but they would not consider guaranteeing the bonds of a railway. He was able to decide that right off because he knew his people and the condition un-
1 a.m. der which they were living.
He knew that the principles of Government of that day would not permit any such thing. Surely the principles of this country will not permit this sort of thing. Where are you going to stop if you give to the Government power to endorse the notes of these people? It is the most outrageous and unreasonable and vicious thing I ever heard of. The Government have no right, in the first place, to juggle with the credit of the Dominion of Canada. When we were asked to vote credits to Boumania and Greece and other countries I opposed the principle then, because I thought the principle was Wrong. I think every member of this House believed it to be wrong at that time, but the Minister of Finance of that day said that the people of Roumania and Greece were crying out for food and that we had to extend these credits to supply them with food and clothing. On the grounds of philanthropy, one might be induced to make a loan to a nation even if you never expect to get the money back, and I never expected that we would in that case, but to endorse notes promiscuously is so foreign to anything a government should do that I am surprised that any serious minded man would consider it for a moment.
Mr. CASGB.AIN: It's a brokers' business.

It is not even a brokers' business. Certainly it is no business for a government or for Parliament. What guarantee have we that if this principle is adopted the Government will not he endorsing the notes of some other people engaged in different industries to-morrow?

What would the hon. gentleman say if he was told the
United States was doing what it is proposed Canada should do?
Mr. 'CAHILL: I would say that it is their business. Even if the United States is doing it, they are in a position to do it. Their money is at par in every country in the world, and above par in a great many countries. Outside of Spain, Japan is the only country in the world where the American dollar is not at par. It was at par in Japan but it is below par there now. The United States is the only country in the world that is on a gold basis possibly with the exception of one or two of the smaller nations. It would be in a position to lend credit or money, but it is not doing it. It has refused to grant any more credits as a government. It is in a better position to do it than we are with our heavy debt and enormous taxes. It was had enough foT the miniate' to come down with his Budget the other day out of which he expects to get money enough* to pay the deficits on our railways. Now he proposes to put an additional burden on the people. Every guarantee you give simply increases the cost of living. There can be no riches produced except those which are produced from the soil, the mine, and from labour which is profitable. If you employ men at something that is unprofitable your labour is wasted. Why try to bolster up any business or industry for which the country is not adapted? If a nation is not able to carry the burden of an industry that is not adapted to it should you not let that industry come to an end? This nation is not in a position, in the face of our debt, to carry on the shipbuilding business on a wholesale scale like some of the European nations, and especially Great Britain. It is a question of trade and you have to do some trading to get something back. You can only trade to the extent of your production, and if y<*u attempt to bolster up a failing industry you are only leading up to a situation which will be worse than it is to-doy and the country will oe in a much graver position than it is at the present time. The people will suffer be' cause they will have to carry the burden. Why should you make loans to, or endorse the notes of, foreigners to buy ships in Canada to compete with our own fleet of ships? It seems to me that the Government has absolutely ignored that argument. I cannot understand why they should insist on bringing in a measure of this kind.
Mr. duTREMBLAY:	These contracts
are taken in France and will be submitted to the Minister of Marine. He is not

obliged to accept a contract if it is not properly carried out. A firm of shipbuilders in France or Spain which would he in a position to give a contract for two or three ships at a cost of $3,000,000 or $4,000,000, will be composed of people who are well known all over the world. If such a contract is given it would be very easy for the Government to find out whether this firm were responsible for the note that they give to the Government. There is also a .question as to the extent to which the mortgage is to be taken by the Government. If I understand the position the Government will not make an advance that will be more than fifty per cent of the value of the contract. Will this contract be a business proposition? The usual cost of a boat is about $1,200,000. Before the Government will be called upon to make any advance they will send some of their architects to the shipyard to find out the progress that, has been made on the work and by that time the shipbuilders from France will have paid to the shipyards in Canada about twenty per cent of the cost of the ship or about $240,000. iCan we suppose that responsible people would pay to a shipyard in this country $240,000 and not continue to make other payments in order that they might receive the ship? It seems to me that Is not possible, as a business matter, that such a firm will not go on with the contract.
This shipbuilding industry was started during the war and there is about $50,000,000 invested in plant in this country. The shipbuilding programme of the Government is about completed, and if we do not receive these contracts -from France and other countries shipyards will have to close. Some of them are nearly closed at the present time. They, have requested the Government for help asking that these companies be subsidized or bon-used to the extent of $15 a ton. The Government has refused to comply with this demand. There is $50,000,000 invested in this industry and there are 25,000 men actually efnployed in these yards and another 25,000 indirectly employed. Everything that goes into a ship can be made in Canada, including the engines and furniture. Is it reasonable when these men have put so much capital in this industry to tell them to-day. "We wall close your doors"? We have been speaking of reconstruction and we must put the country on a good business basis in order that business may be able to meet our requirements. Is this not an important act of reconstruction? Here is a new industry which, if we are able with some little help to make

it permanent, will employ in the future thousands of men and will bring millions of dollars into the country.
I was Speaking, Mr. Chairman, to some men interested in these shipyards and they were telling me that to-day there is the prospect of sufficient contracts to occupy all the shipyards in this country for five years to come. That means hundreds of millions of dollars for this country. The Government will not be responsible and will not be called upon to pay a cent. I do not think the Government are very liberal in their proposition. These shipyard owners went so far as to ask for advances to the extent of 75 per cent to help them finance the work of construction. It is only to aid them in building these ships that this proposition is submitted to Parliament. There is not a bank to-day that is able to finance such an extensive programme as the French Government have submitted to this country. Shall we refuse this opportunity?
This proposition is not a new one. We have protection in connection with the industries of the country, and when we pay customs duties we are paying for that protection. We also give bonuses to certain industries. The Government of the country are elected in order to carry on the country's affairs and it is part of their duty to help to maintain Canadian industries. The farmers should make no complaint; they have been receiving aid for years past, and I am very glad of the fact. In some cases when their crops have failed advances have been made by the Government to help them to tide over the difficulty. The Government have also made loans to farmers. That kind of thing has been done ever since I have had the honour of being a member of the House. I have often been called upon to vote in favour of loaning money to the farmers in the West. Nobody complained because it was thought to be only fair to help that class of the population. Taking all the circumstances into consideration I think it is only fair to help this particular industry, which will contribute so greatly toward the further development of Canada.

I would like to get from the minister some information with respect to the last clause of the resolution, which reads as follows:
Provided that if the vessel is being built for an alien, and the provisions above mentioned with respect to mortgaging the vessel cannot conveniently be complied with, such security for the amount of the said promissory notes endorsed by the Minister of Finance shall be furnished by the purchaser as may be approved by the Governor in Council.

Now there is an "it" in this clause. It has been made clear to the committee that the resolution is intended to find money not for the citizens of Canada or for British subjects. That has been demonstrated by the discussion which has already taken place. Therefore all that part of the resolution which precedes this is of small importance, it is merely a matter of form, and the essence of the thing lies in the last clause. The question then arises, what is the use of talking about a mortgage if you cannot get one. If the situation is such that the property cannot be mortgaged, and there is no security of that kind, why should we continue discussing the- security of a mortgage? That is not what the Government intend; the Government purpose finding some other kind of security because they cannot get a mortgage. We have not had any information from the minister what method he intends to adopt to finance these transactions. If w'e throw the mortgage out of consideration what is it we are going to get? We are going to endorse the note of somebody, and as yet it is all a mystery to me what security we are going to have. A mortgage was the security spoken of. Now it appears the mortgage must be put aside, and we must depend on the Governor in Council to find some other security that will satisfy them in advancing the money.
There is one great objection, in my opinion, to this measure, and that is, using the name of the Dominion of Canada on the notes of any person. I can understand the Government going into the markets of the world, borrowing $30,000,000, and using that money to help the industries of the country; but I cannot understand the country endorsing notes to be floated in the markets of the world which may be defaulted any day and which will go into the hands of a broker to be protested. That is not the way the business of this country ought to be run. My hon. friend from iShelburne and Queen's (Mr. Fielding) has already raised that point. He has stated that if we are going to do business as a country we had better borrow the money and make a clean transaction of it, and not have our name endorsed on notes of the kind that are current in the market. The Prime Minister (Sir Robert Borden) to-day convinced me that we should not pass this legislation. When hon. members on both sides of the House asked that some accommodation be given the soldier fishermen of this conntry, the Prime Minister replied that Canada could not afford to undertake any other liability. He told us that the debt of Canada at the present time was enormous, and that the interest on the debt was equivalent to the revenue we had a few years ago. He told us that the interest on the public debt amounted to $100,000,000, and that while he sympathized with the proposal that something should be done for the soldier fishermen of Canada he could not see his way clear to undertake any further liability. For my part I am going to stand by the Prime Minister.

I really think that the proposition I made to the Government, when I spoke previously, to delay the passing of this resolution until we have sufficient time to look into it, was a fair one. I think the Government should agree to that proposition. Speaking personally, I am not sure that the banks of Canada are not able to advance the $30,000,000 which will be le-quired to float this proposition; and I would like to have time to interview one or two of the bankers to-morrow and find out if the banks cannot advance this money on gilt-edge security. The hon. member for Laurier-Outremont (Mr. DuTremblay) told us that the people who are going to buy the ships are responsible persons, are men of means, and that the Bank of France is behind the transaction. Therefore there should be no trouble in raising the necessary money. I should consequently like to ascertain from our banks if they cannot advance the money, before we decide what we should do with respect to this matter. For that reason we should be given a little time to consider the present resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
There is no intention to hurry hon. members. We would like to dispose of the resolution, and in order that hon. members may have ample time to look into the matter we will not press the Bill to-morrow.
Mr. DU/FF:	If the resolution is carried
all we can do is to amend the clauses of the Bill; the principle of the measure will have been adopted.
No.

That takes place at the
second reading of the Bill.

Why not allow the resolution to stand until to-morrow?-and then we will allow you to advance it. The Prime Minister to-day made the motion that the



business of the House be advanced two stages a day instead of one.
That had reference to private Bills.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I desire to do everything in my power to accommodate the ehon. gentleman. I think he will agree with me that none of us would like to see the discussion take a personal turn. I am quite prepared to consider the suggestions he has made when the Bill is brought down, but I think we should make some progress. My suggestion is that we should now deal with the resolution, and I will then simply introduce the Bill for first reading. Then the Bill will stand over to-morrow with nothing done, and hon. gentlemen will have full opportunity to go into the whole matter on the second reading.
But if we find that the banks will advance money to build ships, then the resolution and the Bill are unnecessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Unfortunately I am sorry to stay that I am in a position to know that it is quite impossible for the banks to do it. The banks have a great many commercial obligations ion their hands now. Commerce within Canada has to be considered. Credits even to-day, as hon. gentlemen know, are being curtailed rather than expanded, and it is right that they should be. Hon. gentlemen must also realize that it takes a great deal of money to properly finance the country's business. With wheat at its present price it takes a very large sum of money to finance the crop, and we ought to do nothing which

will in the slightest degree imperil the proper financing of that crop. The banks are not in a position to take on heavy responsibility in this matter and at the same time look after their obligations to the West.

I cannot agree with the hon. minister in regard to what the banks can do in financing the business of this country. For instance, supposing the fisheries of this country instead of producing $60,000,000 this year produced $120,000,000. would not the banks look after it? Or if our manufacturers could get orders from foreign countries or from our own country for twice their production, would not the banks finance them? It is not a good argument to say that the banks cannot finance the business of this country-and the shipbuilding industry is as important as any other industry. consequently it is a business that the banks must finance just as they finance other business. But if the banks will not finance it, where does the shipbuilder expect to get his money? I say that if he has the proper security the French Government or the Bank of France will accept it. But I feel sure that the shipbuilder can raise the money from the chartered banks of this country, for it must be remembered that this $30,000,000 will be scattered among a number of banks, the shipyards being on the Pacific coast, on the Great Lakes, in Quebec and in Montreal. But, as I said a moment ago, if the banks cannot finance the amount where is the money to come from? It seems to me that before we pass the resolution we should know definitely that it is impossible for the shipbuilders to finance this matter without coming to the Government. Until we are positive on that point I think we certainly should not ask the Government to endorse these notes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. gentleman I know will realize that bank loans are supposed to be liquid, not tied up for two years, which would be entirely against the spirit of the Bank Act.
The banks are doing that every day.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Not very much, and it is not their kind of business. The banks' current business is short-date, as hon. gentlemen well know, usually running for 30 days. The hon. gentleman doubts if there will be any difficulty in financing larger production. I do not know' if the hon.

gentleman had anything to do with the^ difficulties of 1907, but if so he will remember that the grain crop was not financed, and that before the banks would advance money to carry a farmer's grain they first had to be assured of firm contracts for shipment overseas. We have been in that position before, and I can give other instances.

I was quite serious in asking the minister a question about the last clause of the resolution, but I did not receive any answer. It contemplates a case arising in which he cannot get a mortgage. What way is he going to secure the country for a loan if he cannot get a mortgage?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I am sorry I overlooked my hon. friend's question, but after putting it he continued his remarks.
I explained that matter in opening, and I do not know that I can add very much to what I then said. In some alien countries their citizens are allowed to own boats which are not in the register of their country. So 'a boat can be kept in the Canadian registry with a mortgage, and of course the mortgage is not much good unless we keep the boat so registered.
But how can a foreigner give a mortgage on a British ship?
The point, as we all know, is "that the man who owns the ship in Canadian registry must be a British subject. So it is impossible for a subject of France to own a ship in Canada.'

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But the builder certainly can make the mortgage. We have no difficulty about getting the mortgage made. But I understand there is difficulty under the laws of some foreign countries as to their citizens becoming the owners of a boat unless it is brought within the register of their country. If there is that difficulty, as I said in opening, we propose to take security, in the currency preferably of that country, to an amount which will absolutely cover the whole advance with a good margin over and above, and deposit it in the hands of our bankers either in the office of the Bank of Montreal in Paris, France, or in London, England, because in connection with that deposit there is no loss of exchange. If we have to realize on .that in the hands of our agents,, then of course the purchaser would bear the loss on his exchange, but we would be protected.

That
makes your security very doubtful.

The hon. minister says that the ship will be nominally held by the builder, but surely as the purchaser pays for her she becomes his ship. He is at once interested in a British ship, which is against our law, and yet the minister is quite satisfied to take that as security for $30,-000,000-he is willing to take what is nothing more than the defective equity which the foreigner has, in that ship. I would ask the two ministers and the Minister of Justice (Mr. Ddherty), who is at their elbow, what sort of security are we getting? Under our common law the foreigner has no business to own any interest in a British [DOT]ship. Is the Minister of Finance going to take a mortgage on an illegal interest as vested in that owner or held in trust for him by the man who is building the ship? The minister is no better off by taking a mortgage from the man who is building the ship, because he is only holding it in trust for the *other man and what a man cannot himself do he cannot do through a trustee. What sort of security are we getting? I submit that the whole thing is absolutely irregular and, moreover, that this is not the hour of the morning when complicated questions of marine law should have to be put up to the Minister of Justice.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: I understand that under the French law' the Government allows the mortgage on a French vessel to be registered at the port. If the owner were at Marseilles, for instance, the French Government would permit the registry of mortgage at that port.
Question.
Carried.

Oh no, it is not carried. *The Minister of Finance and the Minister of Marine must learn a few lessons, and if there is no other day to bring them to their senses, then we will have to stand in their way as we are doing to-night. Will my hon. friends tell the committee who has made a contract with some builder for the building of a ship? What is the size of the ship? *When is it to be built? We must get down to some shadow of business. I am a much older man than some hon. gentlemen opposite, but I am prepared to sit here until ten o'clock to-morrow, or later, if necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
This does not deal with any specific contract. It is to enable business to be done; and the contracts have to be approved before the business is done. In connection with the other point

the hon. member raises, I admit there are difficulties about mortgaging, and that is why the whole matter is left with the Minister of Justice; he has to be satisfied as to that mortgage. If he is not satisfied, then the pledge has to be made as I explained to the hon. member.

It is quite true, then, that we are in this difficulty from the legal standpoint. If we of the Opposition are beie simply to jump on the band wagon every time the Minister of Finance blows the whistle, we might as well go home. I have been in this House a long time, I was in another House before I came here, I am a trained lawyer and I do not think I should be doing justice to myself or to the people I represent if I allowed this thing to go by. We heard a good deal about some man who was going to make a contract; now we learn that there is no man at all-there is nobody, though the minister seems to think there is some one who will come along. He has his bait out; it is floating along; some fish will bite if the bait is made attractive enough. But nobody will come here to do legitimate business unless we come down with our money. If a man in France wants to build a ship, will he not have it built in England, Scotland or Ireland? Does the minister think that as a business proposition he will come here to get it? The rate of Exchange as between France and England is certainly better than it is between France and Canada. The shipyards are there; the ships can be built at about two-thirds of the cost of building them on this side of the water. There is no business explanation of this proposal. We do not know who wants the ships built; we do not know what the size of the ships will be or how much they will cost. Hon. gentlemen opppsite seem to think this is all nonsense. I see my good friend from New Brunswick (Mr. Loggie) over there. He represents a constituency about as weilthv [DOT] as mine-perhaps not quite so wealthy-and thirty millions is nothing to him and to other hon. members opposite. But if we on this side try to safeguard the people who have to pay the money we are made sport of by hon. gentlemen ooposite. But if my hon. friends are satisfied to take this sweetened pill- if sweetened it is-without anv explanation whatever, then all I have to say is that there will he. a day of reckoning. I know something about the temper of the people of Ontario. We have always hermd members from that province say that they are down on bonuses of any kind; that the farmers of Ontario will not stand for it.

What is the difference between giving bonuses and, giving the whole business, as you are doing here? The whole policy of Ontario on the question of bonuses is being reversed, here to-night; the Government are trying to force down the throats of a few Opposition members a proposal involving $30,000,000. When the Farmers' Party of Ontario understand this situation they will not be very much pleased. Their idea is that every man should do business on his own footing, with his own means and bv his own enterprise. That is the principle upon which this country grew to its present stage. Do not let any one suppose that we have money. We have a little credit left and hon. gentlemen are going to exploit that credit-for whom, we do not know; certainly not for this country. Is this money to be given to any private enterprise that sends a delegation to Ottawa holding out flowerv promises to the Government? We hear that delegations have been coming to this Government dav after day asking for money to start building ships, without, offering anv security except a note without signature and a had stamp on the corner. This is not a good busines proposition and it should not go through.
If the British Empire Steel Company likely to build any of these ships?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I could not give the hon. member any information on that point. I have not heard from them.
Will this be a forerunner of a bonus or bounty for the British Empire Steel Company and other companies of that nature that may come looking to the treasury of Canada ,for support?

Is the British Empire
Steel Company do not own any of the shipyards in Canada, and I doubt very much whether they will.

Do they own the Halifax
shipyard?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
I thought they owned the Dominion Steel Company.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is just a
rumour.

The British Empire Steel
