Company make steel plates, I presume, and they will probably be looking for a bounty fo.r ship plates. If the impression goes abroad that the Government of this country is giving bounties, there is no knowing

what people from all parts of the world will be coming to Ottawa for assistance. They will be getting the impression that the Government of Canada is so easy that all one has to do is to gather up a deputation from some place and bring it to Ottawa and make a demand upon this Government for assistance. As long as the Government had any money to give, these people got the money, and now that they have the money, they are asking for the credit of the country; they are asking the Government to endorse notes. It is well known that a merchant who endorsee anybody's note or notes generally is soon regarded by his banker as a poor risk, and as a general thing a man who endorses notes is not allowed credit by a bank. We have exhausted our money; but our credit is still, to some extent, fair. But if we go on endorsing notes of people who come to us asking for assistance for any kind of undertaking, we shall soon find that not only have we lost our money, but we have lost our credit. A man may lose his money and recover it; but if he loses his credit as well, he is in a very bad position. The Government have not told us why they have adopted this policy; they have not told us where they get their precedent. When they wanted to corner some of the farmers who stated that this was a bad policy, they dug up Saskatchewan, or Alberta, or, perhaps British Columbia. We know what happened in those provinces on account of their guaranteeing bonds, and we know that if the Government of Canada had not. come to the rescue, those provinces would have been in a bad way on that account. Is it the intention of this Government that the Dominion of Canada should get into the same position as the provinces? There is in Ontario scarcely a city or town that has not at some time guaranteed the bonds of, or assisted in some way, some undertaking in the city or town, and what for? Because it is going to employ labour,- and if you employ labour, you are supposed to be doing everything that is necessary. If you go through Ontario, you will find any number of towns which are paying interest on bonds they guaranteed for companies which failed. I do not believe there are half a dozen hon. members opposite-I was going to say one, but they are so erratic, you are liable to find anything amongst them-who would, in their own town, vote to guarantee bonds of any enterprise coming to that town. They will say: No, if this proposition is not good enough to carry on business on its own finances, if this company is not able to finance itself,
we do not believe it is good business to assist it. The same thing applies to a province and still more does it apply to the Dominion of Canada. I doubt very much if any other nation in the history of the world ha6 attempted anything of this kind. I doubt very much if the smallest, the poorest nations of Europe have ever attempted anything of this kind. It is so far removed from the principles of government and out of the line of business of government, that I do not believe there is another nation in the world would attempt this kind of thing. It is the poorest kind of business.
This is very interesting.

If the hon. member is
not interested, why does he not go home?
Mr. EDW'ARDS: I could not tear myself away from the melody of my hon. friend's tones.
As there is an ample number of supporters of the Government present to carry the resolution, one tired member of the House would not make much difference one way or the other.

The hon. member is
mighty poor on jokes.

Quite a number of hon. members opposite might just as well go home because they take no part in the legislation. I can understand their reason for doing so. Nobody except the Government would want to follow this legislation. The Government themselves know they are through, but there are back of them a few members who hope to return to this House again, and they naturally do not want to say anything in favour of this, and I do not blame them at all for that. If my hon. friend (Mr. Edwards) could throw any light on the subject, or if he would even say that he had read the resolution or knows what it is about, it might toe interesting'to allow him to have the floor for a few minutes.

If my hon. friend is directing his 'attention to me, I have no doubt whatever that I.could get up and discuss this subject and any other subject without having it read at all, more intelligently than the hon. gentleman, and I would not be half trying at that,

I know my hon. friend's estimation of himself is so good that he would not need to know even how to read to discuss some subjects as he has done in this House on several occasions to his entire satisfaction. Will the ministry not

give us some idea of where they evolved this bright idea whereby everybody is going to be made rich by taxation, where we are going to continue to build up industry and sell on credit to people who will never pay hack the money? Perhaps, they could give us some idea of what they have in mind-if they have any policy in mind in regard to this guaranteeing of notes of people who may come here for money. Ifxthey refuse to do that, why should they ask us to support this resolution? They should insist on the 'Chairman getting his rest, and should move that the resolution be considered at some other time-perhaps in ten years from now,-a hundred years would be better. I see six ministers in their seats, more than I have seen in the House together almost at any other time this session. Why are there so many ministers here to-night anxious to see this resolution *carried? They have given us no sound reason why this resolution should pass. They have given us no statement of their policy. They have given us no more information in connection with this resolution than they have given us in connection with a great many other resolutions and iBills that have been brought down. I think they should certainly tell us why there is need for all this haste. If it were in order for me to do so, I would move that the committee rise and report progress, but I presume that would not be in order.

I think the minister ought to consider the request of my hon. friend (Mr. Duff) and let us go home and think over this matter before we are required to vote on it. I did not have an opportunity of reading the resolution until the discussion commenced. I have read *it carefully since, but I want to think it over and consult my friends about it. I do not think it is an unreasonable request that we should report progress in order that we may have time to study the resolution. The Minister of Finance has made no reply to this request of my hon. friend, which I think is a very fair and reasonable one. The time thatNvas given to us to look over this resolution before it was moved in the committee was very short indeed. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, only about two months ago, got $20,000,000 from the House for shipbuilding, *and the very same arguments were used then. It was said that the shipyards were going to be idle if we did not vote this $20,000,000 and that 23,000 men would be thrown out of employment. We thought when we 
voted that $20,000,000 a couple of months ago we had settled the' question, for the present session at all events, and it was startling to us to be asked for $30,000,000 more on such short notice. We have plastered this country all over with mortgages during the last two years, and have assumed liabilities of all kinds-$400,000,000 for the Canadian Northern, $400,000,000 for the *Grand Trunk, and so it goes on. When are we going to stop? Does it not alarm even hon. gentlemen opposite? Are they content to go on shingling the country with more mortgages day by day? Are we to be asked to do these things without considering them at all? I think the Minister of Finance will agree with me that this is a rather sudden proposal, and I certainly think we should agree to the request of my hon. friend and move that the committee rise and report progress, so that we may have an opportunity to study this matter more thoroughly.

If we were in the early stages of the session undoubtedly the request of the hon. member (Mr. Duff) would be acceded to, but we are all hoping that we shall get through within a week or ten days. All the Minister of Finance is asking to-night is that the resolution be passed more or less as a matter of form. We are not asking hon. gentlemen opposite to commit themselves to the principle of this resolution at this stage. They will have an opportunity to express themselves on the principle on the second reading of the Bill. All we ask now is that the resolution be passed more or less informally in order to expedite the business of the House. After *the resolution goes through, the Bill will be printed and distributed, and I presume that it will contain provisions that do not appear in the resolution. Hon members will have an opportunity to see the Bill. It is not the intention of the Minister of Finance to press it to-morrow. Every member of the House will have the fullest opportunity of reading its provisions. I fully agree that every member of the House should have the fullest opportunity of examining the legislation from every angle before it is finally put through, and they will *have that opportunity. Every member of the House will also have the privilege of taking any stand he desires on the principle, on the second reading. The Bill will also have to go through the committee stage. So there will be ample opportunity for considering ' this legislation. We are going to have a full day to-morrow, and I think hon. gentlemen might agree to let-

ting the resolution go through now, on division, if desired, on the distinct understanding that they are not committing , themselves on the principle of the resolution, on which every hon. gentleman may take his stand on the second reading of the Bill.
I have not had an opportunity of hearing all the discussion on this resolution, but-
Carried.

If my hon. friends desire to continue their levity, artificial or otherwise, all right. I was going to say that I have not heard all the discussion, but this seems to me a rather serious proposal, and I think it should have been treated with some degree of. seriousness and decorum instead of with the excess of levity and laughter I have heard in the last half hour.
. Mr. EDWARDS: And the silliness from your oiwn side.

I would not be so uncouth as to say there was silliness on the other side. I say this is a matter that hon. gentlemen on this side of the House wish to discuss with what ability they possess. 0.f course we canno t compare in ability with hon. gentlemen on the other side. I have seen the hon. member (Mr. Loggie) beating his desk and throwing back his head [DOT]and laughing for a long while now. I come from the same province and have sat in the same House with him in the province of New Brunswick, and I have never known any one to accuse him of possessing a gigantic intellect. I have no desire to prolong this debate, but I say to the Minister of Finance if he desires to get legislation through the House with expedition he should treat hon. members on this side with some degree of courtesy and decency when they make their arguments.

I have not been doing very much talking, but I have been doing some listening. To some extent I am a protectionist, but my protectionist propensities do not go quite so faT apparently as those of my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Ballantyne). This is protection with a vengeance. During the war when it was necessary to build a few ships the Minister of Marine arranged with the Vickers Shipbuilding institution at Montreal to build those vessels on the basis of paying the cost plus a 65 per cent commission for engaging the help.
Mr. HA LI.AXTYY'K: I never let any contract on a cost-plus basis.
Mr. MoCRELA: Is it not true that the Govt ernment had some vessels built by the Vickers Company and that they paid 65 per cent for employing the labour in addition to 10 per cent for the use of the plant and material?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not this Government.

The previous Government?
<Mr. BALLANTYNEi: I do not know anything about that.

The Borden Government. 1 do not see any difference. I do not know how this will appeal to our new friends at the other end of the Chamber who are opposed to all forms and traditions of protection. It is not only protection hut it is getting vessels built under such circumstances as I have described. I believe in a certain amount of protection, but I think this is carrying it a little too far. The farmers ask the hon. member for Brantfoid (Mjr, Cloickshutt) and others to supply farm implements without any protection at all. I do not know whether he will be in favour of this class of protection. If so he is going a long way to help his fellow manufacturers. I think that shipbuilding is necessary, and it is probably very wise that it should be carried on, hut this is one of the industries that should not go begging in normal times. Before the war freight rates were about one-tenth of what they are to-day. When khips can get rates that they are getting to-day they iare not entitled to a very great deal of bolstering up. We voted the shipbuilding industry $30,000,000 some time ago. Are we going boi vote $30,000,000 more? Does the Minister of Finance realize that he has just adopted a system of taxation under which every little girl on the streets who wears a hat worth two or three dollars is going to pay a tax? We should stop and consider before we vote millions for this class iof industry. There is an arrangement now whereby coal is to be exported from this country in vessels built by the Government, I am in the manufacturing business, and I find it is very difficult to get coal and other material to carry on business with. We are going to bolster up men to build ships to be used for carrying an article out of the country that is very badly needed. I do not believe it is good business. I am in favour of building up all industries that can be build up in this country, but in a country as hard up as we are, in view of

the high rates that are prevailing and in view of the fact that the shipyards thought it was a proper course during the war to exact from the people of Canada 65 per cent commission on labour, it seems to me that it would be well for the Government to stop, think and consider before proceeding with this measure. We on this side of the House ask that it may be allowed to stand over until to-morrow in order that we( may have an opportunity of examining it more closely. I do not think that is asking too much.
Mr. SINCLAIR (Guysborough: How long does the Minister of Marine expect this thing to last? When we voted $20,000,000 recently we thought it would be enough money to carry them along for the present season. The minister has fed the shipyards up with such large contracts for a year or two past that they have got very wealthy. Is this going to be permanent? And, will they come back every year for the same kind of accommodation? That seems to be the hopeless part of the business. The minister has not Told us that this is going to be the last call, for money for these shipyards. There are many shipyards that are not getting any thing out of the bonus th^t is being paid by the Government. We voted $50,000,000 and then $20,000,000, and we are now asked to vote $30,000,000 more. I think we should have some idea as to when this baby is going to get along on its own account. I believe in nourishing the youngster, but when it gets so strong that it wears No. 11 hoots, gets out of the cradle and threatens to kick the GoV(-ernment's blooming head off unless it is given further encouragement, we should find out where the end of it is going to be. I would like to know if this is the last call. We have had this call so frequently that it is alarming. It is alarming my constituents and I submit to the country generally that we are incurring these enormous liabilities time after time. The twenty millions that we have already voted this year for shipyard work is another mortgage on the country. It is adding another $20,000,000 to our debt, and now we have this further proposal. Is this going to stop or is it. going to continue ? Are we to be asked next year for another thirty million in order to keep the shipyards going? I would like the minister to answer that question.

You will kill the audience first.

to expedite this resolution, we want to kill it. The member for Antigonish and Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) a moment ago, put a question to the ministry and they refuse to answer; they sit there dumb. I do not blame them for that. Mr. BALLANiTYNE: I was rising to reply to the hon. member for Guysborough when the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill) intervened.

Very well, I will make
way for the minister now.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member
for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) wants to know how long a period this is for. It is one year. He also wishes to know what the amount involved will be. I do not know what number of ships will be ordered, but if the committee deems it wise the amount can be limited. I said thirty millions; it may be fifteen, or it may only be ten. If the committee wishes a limit to be put, with the consent of the Minister of Finance -with whom I talked just a moment ago -we are willing to limit the amount to $20,000,000, and that will be spread over a. period of three years. A question was also asked as to the size of the ships. The ships will be from 3,750 tons deadweight up to 7,000 tons. If the orders come from France-as I have every reason to think they will-they will be very suitable to our Canadian yards because the lake type of vessels can be used by France as colliers, and the larger vessels can be built in our big yards on both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.

Has the minister any assurance from the shipping people that they will not come back next year for more money? Can the minister assure the committee that he will not require any more money later on to keep the shipyards going, or is he going to ask for money year after year for this purpose? That is the point I am mainly interested in.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hon. member
has been a member of the House much longer than I have been, and I am sure he will agree that he would be an unwise minister that would try to anticipate what might or might not occur a year hence, or at the next session of Parliament. In the words of the late lamented Sir Wilfrid Laurier, "We will have to trust to Providence."
Mr. SINCLAIR- (Guysborough): That is very true, but we are going into a venture that- we ought, to see the end of, and it strikes me that the minister ought to be able to say that in has opinion the shipyards will stand on their own feet if they get the assistance which is being provided for this session, approximating altogether some fifty millions. If he is not able to say so it is a pretty hopeless affair. If these people are not able to live on their own business, and we are to be asked next year to vote more money to keep the shipyards going it is a very sad state of things. The minister ought to be able to see far enough ahead to be able to give some assurance that if we make this large loan to keep the shipyards going for the present year they have some prospect of going ahead on their own account next year.
How many shipyards does the minister consider will be affected by this loan?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Seventeen.
Where are the shipyards?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The hour is late,
still I have no objection to giving the hon. member the information he wants. They are located at Halifax, New Glasgow, Point Levis, Three Rivers (2), Montreal, Port Arthur, Collingwood, Toronto, Midland, Bridgeburg,. Welland, Kingston, Prince Rupert, Victoria and Vancouver (2).

How many shipyards are
in a position to get orders from a foreign country, or from substantial people, if this resolution carries? Will more than one or two be affected?

Has it been tentatively
understood or agreed between the Canadian and French Governments that this business will be forthcoming if the resolution passes?
I have asked the minister whether any other shipyards than one or two will be affected by this legislation?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: As I said before, there are in all seventeen yards. This" matter has been brought to the attention of the Government during the last four months. Various financial groups have waited upon us, and all the shipyards from Piince Rupert to Halifax are very much interested. They are all anxious for business, and they all hope to get it. Beyond that I cannot say.

Will the Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) tell us whether or not this will affect the country's credit? We are borrowing a great deal of money upon which we have to pay interest. We have loans maturing in the United States and in Great Britain, and I have no doubt that we will very shortly have to renew some of them. I would therefore ask the minister, before he asks the committee to pass this resolution, whether he thinks it will in any way affect the credit of the Dominion?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The power is
taken for the Government to control the discount in place of paying for these notes. We are not allowing the notes to be hawked around as has been suggested by one hon. member. Of course we have got any amount of liabilities to meet-and I think we are going to meet them. But there is one thing we have all got to bear in mind, that the only way to meet our liabilities is to carry on, and that it is not a very good thing'when we are keeping shop and meeting our liabilities to have a large amount of unemployment in an important industry.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to tender a mild protest. I asked a question of the hon. minister twice, but no answer has been forthcoming. Now, although the*ant cannot push the elephant, it objects to being pushed by the elephant, and I think that if my question was courteously put-and I meant it to be-I should be accorded some sort of answer. I would like to have an answer to the one question I put to the minister.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think that question was put to the Minister of Marine and

Fisheries, but evidently he did not hear it, because he has just asked me what it was. The question was whether the Government of France were interested in this matter. Whether that government, as a government, is interested I do not know, except to this extent, that the gentlemen who have presumably been interested on behalf of the French Government wanted to get credits for the purpose of shipbuilding. Further than that, offers were made at one t;me by those gentlemen that they would supply bonds of the French Government for the full expenditure, and of course if they had done that undoubtedly the French Government would have to be interested. I cannot speak about it personally because I did not follow it up.

The question that I wished answered was whether, in the information of the Government, the French Government would be disappointed, as a result of the communications that have passed between the two governments, if this resolution does not carry?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We cannot say whether the French Government would be disappointed or not, but I m.ay say that they are intensely anxious that this matter should go through. A proposition was made to us to take French bonds, but other conditions were attached that did not satisfy the Government. I should judge from the negotiations that went on for some time that the French Government are very much interested.

I gather from the statements of the minister that he is not in the same position as when shipbuilding himself, for then he had control of the money; but in this case he has no control over the money at all, he simply endorses a certain document which enables the man building the ship to get the money and pay it out. If we iwere giving a bounty we would know we were giving so much a ton and would not expect to get it back, except indirectly in the way of increased industry. Another objection to this proposal is that the man in France in getting his ship built will surely take advantage of the market, and if he is a business man at all he will call for tenders in the open market and get shipbuilders from the Old Country to underbid us every time, because they are able to build ships very much cheaper than we can, with the result that we will have to make some business losses in order to secure any contracts.

I may say, Mr. Chairman, that I was never more honest than in my opposition to this resolution to-night. I am honestly convinced that the Government should not have introduced this resolution, that it should not pass the House, and that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House should refuse to give their assent to an expenditure of this kind. We were told in the early stages, in the suave and positive manner of the Minister of Finance, that he had the most ample security for the money he was paying out, but when we came down to a little closer investigation we found he was getting no security. That foreigner is too cute for the minister. The foreigner has the ship and cannot give a mortgage on it, and therefore my hon. friend has no security. He has failed to tell us where the other security is to come from. We thought at one time that it would be on the ship, but it has been abundantly demonstrated that a foreigner cannot own a ship in this country. Perhaps if the minister gives this matter fuller consideration he will be able to satisfy himself that he cannot get any security, and that therefore as 'trustee of the money of the people he had better not press this proposal to a conclusion under present circumstances.
Where does the company buying the ship and for whom the note is endorsed expect to get the money? Do they expect to finance it with the Canadian banks?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No, not the Canadian banks; that will be left with us to arrange. The- Government prefers to attend to that. We will not finance it in such a way as to make any conflict with our own banks or take any of our necessary money out of the country.
What has the Government in mind as to how the financing will be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It will be financed in whichever market is the best; at the moment the chances are it would be the American market.
You will state where the company which has the 'note may dispose of it; so that it is really equivalent to a short-term Canadian bond. That is whiat it amounts tioi.
Does this resolution apply only to existing contracts, or will it apply also to contracts made in the future?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It does not apply to any particular contract. It will apply to any proper contract.

The minister has given as the main reason for this resioilution the suggestion that the shipbuildng industry in Canada needs help. If the resolution applied only to existing contracts there might be some reason for it; but why open the door to all contracts in the future? Any man who goes into the shipbuilding business may take advantage of this legislation and obtain help from the Government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It merely applies to existing shipyards. In the case of any existing shipyard with a force of men employed, it would apply to any contract necessary for the purpose of keeping it going.

Is it the intention of the Government to bring down, based upon this resolution, a general Bill, or will the Bill be restricted as to its clauses? Will there be a preamble explaining the reasons for the introduction of the Bill?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There will not be a general Bill. It will be a Bill for a specific purpose, but it will limit the amount.

The principle of the Bill is most extraordinary and exceptional. That the Government of this country khould step in and help a particular industry is something new. I do not think that the principle is good. I believe that the House would look with more favour upon a Bill in which the primary reasons for its introduction were stated than it would upon a general Bill without any explanations or restrictions.
Resolution carried on division, reported and concurred in.
Sir HENRY DRAYTON (Minister of Finance) thereupon moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 199, to assist shipbuilding.
Motion agreed to and Bill read the first time.
On motion of Rt. Hon. Mr. Doherty the House adjourned at 2.42 a.m. (Wednesday) .
